Il y a des jeux que l'on termine.

Et il y a des jeux auxquels on revient.

XCOM 2 fait partie de ceux-là.

Ce n'est pas seulement un excellent jeu de stratégie au tour par tour. C'est une formidable machine à créer des histoires. On ne se souvient pas uniquement des missions, mais des soldats qui les ont vécues.

On se rappelle d'un rookie devenu colonel contre toute attente. D'un sniper qui réussit un tir impossible. D'un Ranger qui se sacrifie pour permettre à l'escouade de s'échapper. Ou de ce vétéran que l'on attend impatiemment pendant des semaines à l'infirmerie.

Peu de jeux créent un tel attachement à leurs personnages.

War of the Chosen sublime encore l'expérience. Les factions, les Élus, les nouvelles mécaniques stratégiques et la gestion de plusieurs escouades donnent une profondeur incroyable à la campagne. Chaque décision compte, et les conséquences se font sentir pendant des dizaines d'heures.

Mais ce qui fait entrer XCOM 2 dans une catégorie à part, c'est sa communauté.

Près de dix ans après sa sortie, des moddeurs passionnés continuent d'enrichir le jeu avec de nouvelles cartes, classes, ennemis, systèmes de progression et améliorations de qualité de vie. Au point qu'il est possible de façonner une campagne presque sur mesure, sans jamais trahir l'esprit du jeu d'origine.

Peu de jeux peuvent se vanter d'une telle longévité.

Pour moi, XCOM 2: War of the Chosen reste tout simplement la référence du jeu tactique moderne au tour par tour. Chaque nouvelle campagne raconte une histoire différente, et c'est probablement sa plus grande force.

Un chef-d'œuvre du genre.

The game seems great, it's just really not for me; this is a situation where I can't recommend it due to my own taste, nor do I want to tell fans of this genre to outright avoid it.

It's story telling within the small amount of time i've played, is spot on with lots of proper voice acting and world building- some parts doing a little too much "telling" rather than "showing," that being a small gripe.

XCOM 2 also includes a whole base/headquarters system where you can research, craft and manage resources, which in my opinion is a great touch and would have loved exploring the available possibilities that come a little later in the player's progression.

My main complaint:
I came into this assuming it was a CRPG, considering the turn based mechanics and a team you build and control. It does showcase a lot of what makes it to be, but the main discrepancy being the characters you control, are all capable of dying permanently in 1 - 2 RNG shots (early on but could also be later on too?), as well as not being able to build them through a stat sheet. I don't mind the exclusion of a modifiable stat system, as it's mainly handled by equipment and levels, but I do dislike the fact that it can all disappear because of 1 simple mistake or bad RNG. It didn't seem like there was any counter play for when a member of your team dies other than continuing the game while recruiting another expendable character, restarting the mission, or save scumming.

There's a lot of praise for this game, I truly believe the experience is great and worthwhile due to the communities' opinion. Going into this expecting the possibility to create your own team that you could stick with the entire time, and that there would be counterplays to possible permadeath, ruined the experience for me. I can't refund it because I bought it long ago, but I'll most likely give this one another try later down the line, now knowing what to expect.

X-Com 2 [WotC, as I've not played vanilla] is a very good game. It starts off very difficult, as the tutorial is... lacking, and the difficulty is the highest when you don't know the enemy, don't have many options to recover from mistakes and most importantly lack the experience to exercise proper judgment. Once you learn it a little, the game becomes easier, though the game does love throwing surprises at you at first encounters with an enemy (like the Muton counterattack, Andromedon suit revival or Sectopod explosion). Once you learn it more, the game gets quite a bit of depth, mostly due to the destructible environment. Block one ladder and destroy another, force a Hunter to break his legs repeatedly, Remote Detonate a train to cause a nuclear explosion after the enemy used it for cover, blow up the walls of a facility to access it easier, the possibilities are varied. Additionally, late in the game, there are just more tools available for tactical flexibility than earlier, like grapples, death from above, inspire, stasis and more, compared to just using a grenade to blow up a tree early on.

The Chosen are decently fun to fight. Knowing that they don't start their attacks until they're in actual fighting range is integral and, of course, not mentioned anywhere in the game. Spamming Mind Control is annoying, getting crit-bonked or bled out is also annoying, but not uncounterable... usually. The Rulers are bosses in every sense, when they actually attack, they deal the damage of a medium-high threat enemy, but with one action taken for every nearly one of XCOM's actions (Including ones that are not offensive or straight up miss). Devastate and Quake are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, Icarus Kidnap or whatever it's called is difficult to counter and why the hell do bosses that don't take cover have such high defense? I'd still recommend turning on the random mission Rulers, they make the game significantly more varied. The Lost, I could do without, honestly. Being punished for explosions, including ones I have no control over, is BS and they aren't even that threatening. The Twin Towers is negated by bluescreen rounds and is a long slog, even if it gives a SPARK and a lot of AP. The Nest, I did once. Central, I wish you stayed in that cave instead of yapping about AVATAR. 

Skirmishers are fun, but weak - their skills are good, their weapons are not. Reapers are fun and strong, in spite of their long-range highly-accurate peashooter weapon. things have changed a lot since 2014 in terms of what i consider acceptable from a tactics game. at a bare minimum i expect the UI to accurately reflect what will happen when I click a button, or offer confirmations for important, irreversible actions. i also expect that if you want your game to look nice, you first make it systemically robust and not obscure crucial information for the sake of aesthetics.

there is a system in this game which tells you if a move will break cover, but it's not always accurate. even if no warnings are showing, it's possible that a move will clip the corner of a watched tile, or move into the LOS of an enemy which you don't know about and thus don't have warnings for. i can accept the reasoning behind the latter, but it's also not clear which tiles are in "fog of war" and which are just dark, so it's impossible to know where enemies could be. any move can result in breaking cover and you have no way of knowing, which could be intentional but just feels oppressive to me.

the game is really 3d, with multiple height levels and detailed scenery, all of which can be used as cover or destroyed. there are also frequent bugs with this system as characters can noclip melee and shoot through walls as though they didn't exist. sometimes the visual placement of a character model implies something other than their actual cover / LOS status. shots that seem to clearly be possible are actually blocked, parsing which tiles will allow you to shoot an enemy is difficult, and knowing the chance of hitting from any given tile is impossible without committing to move there.

I finally quit when a soldier running up onto a building was spotted by an enemy I had vision on and no warning that my move would break cover. Then a snake inside that building clipped its tongue through the wall and pulled her inside. the aliens then had perfect information on where my squad was and mostly killed me on their next turn.

you can abuse some of these issues to your own benefit but it doesn't feel fair. it's always possible that i'm just bad, but when I break cover or lose a soldier it never feels like i made a tactical mistake. it just feels like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

Un joc turn-based foarte bun. 

Povestea are loc dupa evenimentele din primul joc, unde dupa tot chinul din X-COM 1 Enemy Unknown omenirea a pierdut razboiul impotriva extraterestrilor. Pamantul este acum controlat de ADVENT, o organizatie care pretinde ca lucreaza pentru binele oamenilor, dar in realitate ascunde planurile extraterestrilor. Tu conduci din nou organizatia X-COM, care acum opereaza ca o miscare de rezistenta si incearca sa elibereze planeta.

Gameplay-ul este excelent si fiecare misiune te pune sa gandesti fiecare mutare. Nu este genul de joc in care alergi direct spre inamici. Pozitionarea, folosirea adapostului, abilitatile soldatilor si gestionarea echipei sunt foarte importante. Chiar si un soldat experimentat poate muri din cauza unei singure decizii proaste, iar asta face fiecare victorie mult mai satisfacatoare.

Un lucru care mi-a placut foarte mult este personalizarea soldatilor. Le poti schimba aspectul, numele, vocea si echipamentul, iar dupa cateva ore ajungi sa te atasezi de ei. Tocmai de aceea, atunci cand unul moare permanent pe campul de lupta, chiar simti ca ai pierdut ceva important.

Pe langa misiuni, trebuie sa gestionezi si baza mobila Avenger. Cercetezi tehnologii noi, construiesti camere, antrenezi soldati si alegi ce obiective sa prioritizezi. La inceput pare mult de invatat, dar sistemul este intuitiv in 10 minute ai prins schema si contribuie foarte mult la progresul campaniei.

Jocul poate fi si frustrant. Celebrul procent de 95% sanse de lovire care rateaza exact cand ai cea mai mare nevoie a devenit aproape un meme in comunitatea X-COM. Uneori simti ca jocul este impotriva ta, dar tocmai aceasta tensiune face fiecare misiune memorabila.

It's XCOM baby

The base game is already an incredible turn based strategy game. Every mission feels meaningful because every decision matters. Positioning, ability usage, resource management, and even a single missed 95% shot can completely change the outcome. (Yes, it will miss. It always misses.)

What really makes it special is how attached you become to your squad. They're not just units on a battlefield. They're your sniper who's survived since the first month, your Ranger who somehow keeps carrying impossible missions, and your Specialist who always seems to be one turn away from disaster. When someone dies, it actually hurts because you know exactly what it took to get them there.

Then there's War of the Chosen, which somehow takes an already fantastic game and makes it even better. The Chosen constantly keep you on your toes, the faction heroes introduce entirely new playstyles, covert actions make the strategy layer far more engaging, and the Bond system gives your soldiers even more personality. It doesn't feel like an expansion. It feels like the definitive version of the game. (Which it basically is since you have to launch it separately.)

While the game is no longer receiving official support, you honestly don't notice because the modding community has kept it alive in a way very few games ever achieve. The Steam Workshop is absolutely packed with mods. Quality of life improvements, new classes, new enemies, new maps, cosmetic options, complete gameplay overhauls, and even entire new campaigns. You can tweak the experience just a little or completely reinvent it into an entirely different game. It's one of the strongest modding communities I've ever seen, and it's a huge reason why people are still playing years later.

The amount of replayability is ridiculous. Different squad compositions, research paths, campaign modifiers, and thousands of community mods mean no two campaigns ever feel exactly the same. Even after hundreds of hours, I still find myself saying, "Just one more mission."

My only real complaint is the removal of multiplayer. Since the official servers are gone, the multiplayer achievement is no longer obtainable through normal means. If you're an achievement hunter like me, you'll need to install a community mod that restores multiplayer functionality just to unlock it. It's a small part of the overall experience, but it's unfortunate that completionists have to rely on the community for something that used to be built into the game.

Pros:
- Outstanding tactical combat
- Every decision feels meaningful
- Soldiers become characters you genuinely care about
- War of the Chosen is one of the best expansions ever made
- Incredible replayability
- One of the best modding communities on Steam
- Thousands of mods that keep the game feeling fresh

Cons:
- Official multiplayer support has been removed
- Multiplayer achievement now requires a community mod
- Missing a 95% shot will permanently alter your trust in statistics

in 2025 i spent the most turbulent year of my life. i didn't mean to, but the turbulences made their way to me and i accepted them with open arms, as if it were mere expected disturbances on a plane. it was most likely the first and last year i have ever experienced true love. it was also the year i played XCOM 2 most.

at first, it was a hunch - "i may enjoy this, i always liked the idea of turn based combat, never had the money to try this at launch when i was a kid, how does it feel to play this?" it instantly got rid of that itch i had in my retarded brain for years on end after i saw a preview of the gameplay. the campaign felt so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good i couldn't stop playing. work and chores became secondary to whatever wizardry was at play in this title. i wasn't hooked, i was high as a kite on an endless supply of free dopamine from XCOM 2. i made characters that i was emotionally attached to, played around with mods, kept my eyes glued to the screen during every majorly meaningful single digit percent shot. i was fully invested and became a fangirl in days.

i don't touch upon this title nowadays, mainly because for the last half a year i tried to repress the idea of *him*, my most likely last ever love, out of my head. but undeniably, I can't.

his existence in my life overlapped with my love for XCOM 2 and many other steam titles. when i loved a game, he was first to know. when i was frustrated with a puzzling element of any game, he was first to sit beside me with a solution. when a game made me tear up, he was first to brush off my tears. we loved gaming. we would do it for days. it was our thing beside being lovers of soviet culture, psychology, music, kink, survivalism, the military, weaponry and philosophy.

we were born with neural systems that were never meant to collide at the time they did. we were raised with backgrounds that were sure to mismatch. we spent countless hours discussing, trying to figure it out, and then many hours arguing in frustration, then few hurting eachother, sometimes without even knowing. modern life didn't accept our kind and filtered us through its tiny holes, fast. we ground eachother down and I haven't seen him or even heard him speak since the last time i decided that in spite of how much i wanted, i couldn't.

in late 2025, i crossed him off, and with him i crossed off many memories, photos, habits, and alongside those - games. i abandoned XCOM2 for some time. i have attempted to date again and found myself in an actual workplace relationship for about 3 months, but i would lie if i said i loved any of those men. i haven't said the words "i love you" to anyone i have dated since *he* left. i am afraid of this sentence altogether. when the words were said to me, for the first time in my life, i ran. i did something i never thought i would and, just like *he* would at times (and by proxy - taught me how to do), i ran away from love. i still do it. i might never stop because of how comfortable it feels to run away.

when i painstakingly finished XCOM2, i felt empty. not because it was over, but because *he* wasn't there anymore to talk to me about it. i couldn't be autistic to anyone about it anymore. there isn't really anyone around i would tell about it. but XCOM 2 was and is and will always be nostalgic to me - not because i got to play it as a child or a teen, but because after years of craving it I got to finally play it. just like after years of searching, i finally found him.

i may never speak to him again, i may one day fall in a fraction of love i felt for him, but i might love what i remember of him forever. i still crave the kids we could've had, who could've gotten to play all the katamari damacy, disco elysium, XCOM that they wanted. i still wish i could play XCOM 2 again the first time, to try and love him better the first time. but i can't. and i hold onto the memory of the title, and of *him*, as the essence of when i was happy. in spite of it all.

i will pretend until i die that i hate him, that the pain he inflicted upon me is an obstacle to my happy existence, but I'm not angry anymore. last time i checked, at the end of 2025, he was happy with someone else. and that's all that matters, really. our separation and my longing for the endless blue of his eyes is a good thing. i will remember him not for the times he ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up, when i ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up, when he couldn't control whatever patterns and fear he inherited, but for the love he gave. for the spaghettis, the lovemaking, the shopping, the protection, the midnight psychoanalysis, the way he played the guitar, his smell, his hair, his humour, his calm, his strenght, his shape, his melancholic sense of self. i will remember him for how he tried, not for how he failed. i choose to repress the wrongs because i know no one else will dwell upon them. i am in love with someone, but he isn't here, and i think that's okay. this is right.

Edit: TLDR: XCOM 2 isn't remotely difficult, it's merely punishing. And the things it punishes the player for feel completely arbitrary in a game that is entirely balanced around the AI being utterly incompetent.

Astoundingly sloppy. I considered this a well-regarded series, but I'm a bit surprised that people are willing to settle for this. The writing is utilitarian genre drivel, though that's typically what you might expect for a tactical game like this. The gameplay is the real focus. Unfortunately, XCOM 2 really ♥♥♥♥♥ the bed in this regard as well.

Depending on who you ask about it, you will hear both that XCOM 2 is brutally difficult and laughably easy. The latter is probably more true given enough experience with the thing. Because the game is dependent on a random number generator (RNG) to determine the outcomes of actions, the combat is incredibly swingy. Whether an attack hits or misses has a huge impact on the rest of the encounter (and the overarching campaign by extension). Therefore, it is paramount to mitigate the RNG whenever possible, generally resulting in one specific course of action being optimal. This won't prevent extremely frustrating outcomes, but "That's XCOM, baby!" The gameplay is actually pretty fun (for a time) once you get past the initial hurdle of the game doing an incredibly poor job of communicating things to the player. There are a lot of factors to keep track of, and Firaxis' methods of tutorializing are at once egregiously tedious and yet somehow insufficient.

The real issues arise as you become more and more aware of how badly implemented most of the gameplay is. AI behavior is extremely predictable given even the blandest of circumstances. Enemies really only pay attention to whether you're in cover and whether they can hit more than one target with an AoE (area of effect) ability. As a result the game quickly becomes aggressively boring once you're familiar with each enemy type, and no amount of arbitrary difficulty can fix that.

Additionally, Firaxis puts their thumb on the scale in order to offset behavioral programming limitations. For example, when you are in concealment, the AI will gradually "patrol" over to you and simply stand there, locking down one or more of your squadmates as they wait for you to break stealth. The AI knows where you are (as if there isn't a more elegant way to balance a mechanic that the devs opted for), and this completely breaks immersion. Honestly, the whole "pod" system for enemy distribution feels horribly "gamey." I'm sure there are plenty of people that this won't bother, but when I become too aware of an artist's/creator's deliberate machinations, my suspension of disbelief falls apart.

Did I mention the game is really buggy? Like... inexcusably buggy (on top of having a generally clunky interface). I am constantly waiting for bugged animations to time out, surprised by a teammate or enemy having X-Ray vision, or loading a save because a squad member moves somewhere that I emphatically did not tell them to move. 

Rather than create a holistic system for intuitive gameplay and engaging encounters based on enemy behaviors (which is an opportunity for storytelling), Firaxis is really just curating a set of narrativizable experiences that follow predictable prescribed courses. It's a toybox. Sure, novel things do happen. Sure, you can exercise some creativity to great effect, but the possibility space for both of those aspects is severely limited by the devs' utter lack of ambition. It's like all they could think to do was add more mechanical impositions (and tiresome cinematic animations). They shot for mediocre and by god they succeeded. I remember liking Enemy Unknown more, but I couldn't say how well it's aged. Not everyone is going to share my objections, and there is a good amount of fun to be had here. I just can't recommend it.

Got this game at launch. It was awesome then, before any DLC or patches. And this has been one of the rare games in my experience where everything just got better with it. To the extent that sure, you can get the base game and have a great time with it. But the DLCs are true DLCs and actually add worthwhile content that helps flesh out the game in ways where there wasn't anything there before. I am not even going to mention the mods beyond that they do nothing but the same and take it even further. This is a beautiful turn based tactical that has a ton of attention to detail on it. From the basic personal profiles on each of your soldiers to the propaganda posters you can make for fun a then end of your missions being able to be randomly found within the same campaign in random missions later on. And if that wasn't enough of an example of attention to detail, the exact same system not only creates a local copy for you for EACH poster but also has a hot button in game that you can click that will open windows explorer and take you to the poster in question within that folder.

Even something as simple as the main menu, they could've done something bland or basic with an image or some randomly animated background. But instead they load a random scene based of your latest save. Usually this is one of my highest ranking soldiers and its as if it is mid-turn you just took the camera and put it over their shoulder. There isn't an exact loop this either beyond the soldier's individual animation loop of just standing there hiding. But its still really cool to see this kind of innovation for something so simple and when most developers would do something far more basic. And there are details of this level throughout the entire game to enjoy.

Sure this game does have a couple of flaws, the aim logic can be questionable at times, the camera angles get a little wonky every  now and then where you're watching a wall while something happens, and I have had a few crashes during my ten years of playing this game. But these aren't regular occurrences for me as I've had only about 5 that I can recall in total and mind you this is with dozens, if not a few hundred mods loaded.

If you're curious there is plenty of gameplay footage on youtube by this point. But if it is any consolation the screenshots on the store page are directly from the game and not filtered. It really just looks that good in game. 

At this point all I can say is that I have high hopes for XCOM 3 and that the developers exceed them.

Also glad this game has more heft to it than the first game so i felt i had a satisfying amount of playtime.

The game also has a bit more story to it though it can be a bit few and far between and I wasn't too invested. Game felt a bit too easy by the time you get end game abilities and gear and it kinda wore out its welcome. Missions started to feel kinda repetitive and the March to the end had lots of waiting around. By the end of the game your units get exhausted and mentally fatigued so easily which just feels like an artificial limitation to counter your imported healing facilities which just feels like you made no progress. Also maybe not the best streaming game as I sometimes reloaded saves to avoid taking a back breaking loss for the sake of making sure I finish the game in a timely manner. A solid tactics game that improves upon the modern xcom formula with a cool premise that gets a little long in the tooth by the end.

The endgame is much easier than the early game which seems backwards but makes sense with you overthrowing the whole alien dictatorship, the chosen get outpaced really easily but at least get ceremonial deaths and the final confrontation is set up really well. XCOM 2 is probably one of the best, if not THE best turn-based tactical strategy games out there. With a small bit of base building and more macro strategy elements mixed in there. You really do feel rewarded for learning more about the game, with each mission giving you something new to think about and a new way to take on missions.

I do have my gripes, however. Some of the content does feel a little bit rushed, and there are a few bugs (do NOT alt-tab. The game is not friendly to it, and at one point it damn near burst my ear drums with static), however the game feels pretty well optimised and runs fantastically.

There's enough enemy variety, map variation, mission differences, and XCOM operative class variety to keep you entertained throughout a run through, and the amount of replayability is amazing. If you've been thinking about getting XCOM 2 to try it out, then please do! Check out the mod market too, the amount of mods to customise your characters and the enemy makes each run feel very fresh. Overall, I'd really recommend XCOM 2 if you're looking to scratch a specific itch

I remember that happened during my first fight with an Andromedon. If you look past the math, and view the game as a simulation of combat, it is much more fun than pulling hair over numbers. I recommend not using Ironman with mods, but reloading saves outside of being soft-locked is a waste of your time and denies you the opportunity to learn from your mistakes. Don't always take the highest percentage shot, make the best choice. Retreat if needed, discretion is the better part of valor. Try not to rush, but moving swiftly is necessary. Adapt your strategy to the situation, learn from experience when to spread out and when to consolidate. However, soldiers who fight alone often fall alone. I believe going in blind without watching other people play is the most interesting way to experience a game like this. Checking the settings for extra controls on shortcuts can be helpful. Good luck, commander.

XCOM 2 is a lot of things to a lot of people.

For some it's a save scumming, light alien adventure with a rag-tag group of 6-15 operatives throughout the whole game. For some it's a difficult turn based strategy game where you feel the weight of building a group of 20-30 soldiers and tackle the alien menace. For others it's a Star Wars X Every Fortnite Skin 100+ hour warfare with 1000s of soldiers training, fighting, and dying for the cause.

That is to say this game has a lot of versatility, and your milage will vary with how close you can manage to get this game to align with the type of experience you're looking for.

I don't think there's been a better customizable alien war strategy game released in the decade since XCOM 2 came out.

A must-play for fans of turn-based strategy games. The balance between base management, research priorities, resource allocation, and battlefield operations is excellent, constantly forcing difficult decisions in the fight against the alien threat.
The story is fairly minimal, but that's clearly not the focus. Instead, the game shines through its strategic depth and the relentless technological arms race that pushes players to adapt or risk falling behind. This pressure can sometimes feel oppressive, and the game is unforgiving when missions go wrong, but learning from failures and refining your tactics is where the experience is at its best.
While combat is often criticized for being luck-based, success ultimately comes down to risk management and maximizing favorable odds. That said, no discussion would be complete without mentioning those infamous missed 98% shots that turn victories into disasters and create some of the most memorable moments the genre has to offer.

I loved the game, it is definitely better than the first one. A true sequel that's better in every way.

Although, I didn't really like the "resistance"-theme this time around, the plot was also okay.

I have to say though - I've only finished the campaign on something like a medium or standard difficulty and called it a day. This definitely doesn't do the game justice, because it can and should be played more. It's just I have a huge backlog and I want to move through it somehow.

But, if you're interested, there's also a ton of mods and a huge community.

I would say that close competitors are definitely Phoenix Point, which I played actually after I finished XCOM Enemy Within and before XCOM 2. That game may not be as polished as this one, but PP definitely does a few things better than XCOM 2, specifically when it comes to warring "allied" factions and diplomacy between them. It also felt more dauting and survival-like. 

Another close competitor, I would say is Battletech. Yeah, I know it's pretty different with mechs and all, but it's close enough for me with the crew and ship management. It feels a bit more open-ended with a lot more player agency.

Finally, I can't not mention Xenonauts 2, which is what XCOM 2 would have been if it had the original developers, or so I think. That game is the very essence of what XCOM is and a lot more complex.

But yeah, XCOM 2 is a great game and it definitely stands the test of time.

 В моем случае наиграно не так много часов, но чтобы сделать какой-то вывод о данном шедевре, я запас пару интересных мыслей о ней, и с "удовольствием" поделюсь ими с вами. 
 Начнем с того что, если вы играли в великолепную XCOM: Enemy Unknown / Within и ждете от сиквела честной военной тактики, где жизнь каждого элитного бойца спецназначения — это высший приоритет, а экономика работает на снабжение фронта, то забудьте. Вторая часть — это не тактика. Это душный симулятор борьбы с ленивым геймдизайном, завернутый в клише фантастики 90-х.

ПЛЮСЫ:
1. Атмосфера партизанского сопротивления. 
На бумаге идея «мы проиграли войну и партизаним на угнанном корабле» звучит круто и стильно.
2. Механики фракций из DLC. 
 Жнецы с их невидимостью и детонаторами, а также Заступники действительно вносят разнообразие в унылый стоковый геймплей, а он унылый, кто бы что не говорил. Они выпустили это ДЛС только для того, чтобы разнообразить карты, противников, добавить союзников и в целом, я так понял, втихую чуть забалансить игру, потому что их травмированный жест былых времен(вот раньше было лучше) - явно никто не оценил.

С плюсами все, думаю тут многого и не скажешь.

МИНУСЫ:
1. Искусственная сложность вместо интеллекта врагов. 
 Разработчики не смогли сделать искусственный интеллект пришельцев умным. Вместо этого они усложнили игру тем, что скрутили игроку руки. Сложность растет не от хитрых маневров врага, а от того, насколько сильно вам зажали яйца в тиски ограничений. Карманы бойцов обрезаны: вы физически не можете положить боевому товарищу в инвентарь и гранату, и копеечный ментальный щит от гипноза одновременно. Выбирай: или ты взрываешь стены, или твой боец сходит с ума. Это все даже на мизерном, лоховском(как сказали бы, я уверен, фанаты этой игры, именно этой игры, а не вселенной) уровне сложности. К тому же, чем выше сложность игры, тем все сильнее ресурсы и время, драгоценное ваше время в игре - становится под расчет, никто не даст вам фармить точки на карте сколько вам это нужно, через пару, или пару-тройку(дай Бог) дней вас убедительно попросят выдвинуться на задание по спасению какого то е%%на, потому что это КРИТИЧЕСКИ важно для СОПРОТИВЛЕНИЯ, и вот вы уже понимаете, что с прошлого задания все ваши бойцы либо погибли(зачастую), либо ранены и взять их не получится, настало время героев современности - Новобранцев).

2. Маразм игровой экономики и интерфейса.
 Игра заставляет вас играть в бухгалтерский менеджмент нищеты. У вас на базе летает гигантский хайтек-корабль, работают лучшие умы планеты, но чтобы выдать бойцу карманную аптечку или улучшить автомат, вам нужно лично гриндить ресурсы и собирать ржавые гвозди по помойкам. При этом интерфейс откровенно держит игрока за дебила: во вкладке производства Наножилет (+1 ХП, сующийся в слот вместо гранаты) покупается поштучно и стоит как крыло самолета, а нормальная броня «Хищник» имеет плашку [УЛУЧШИТЬ: ОТРЯД]. Но из-за дебильного визуала новичок уверен, что ему придется спонсировать каждого солдата отдельно, из-за чего совершает критические ошибки в развитии базы. Я хочу подметить, игра не для новичков вселенной, чтобы начать играть в нее условно с этой части, вам нужно знать, что было в прошлой, не потому что сюжет связан(хотя и поэтому тоже), а потому что механики все оттуда перекочевали. Даже при выборе уровня сложности вам говорят - ВЫ УВЕРЕНЫ, ЧТО ХОТИТЕ ОТКЛЮЧИТЬ ОБУЧЕНИЕ? Да бл;%%%ь уверен, Боже... И это будет критическая ошибка опять же для новичка, но я думаю они и не нажмут ее, хотя кто его знает.

Le genre de jeu qui m'a fait passer par toutes les émotions possibles. Satisfaction, stress, soulagement, frustration, beaucoup de frustration, parfois même un profond sentiment d'injustice. Et pourtant, malgré les crises de nerfs qu'il peut provoquer, c'est probablement l'un des meilleurs jeux de stratégie tactique auxquels j'ai joué.

Le plus appréciable dans XCOM 2, c'est sa capacité à faire croire que chaque décision compte. Quand un soldat survit à plusieurs missions, monte en grade et commence à accumuler les exploits, il cesse rapidement d'être une simple unité sur une grille. On finit par lui attribuer une personnalité, à retenir ses actions héroïques ou ses erreurs catastrophiques. Du coup, quand une mission tourne mal, les conséquences ont un véritable poids. Chaque soldat a le potentiel de devenir le héro de guerre qui vous restera en tête après la fin du jeu.

Les combats sont excellents. Le système est facile à comprendre mais difficile à maîtriser, et le jeu réussit constamment à mettre le joueur sous pression. Entre les objectifs chronométrés, l'infériorité numérique, les renforts ennemis et la nécessité d'avancer rapidement, on ne peut presque jamais se contenter d'attendre derrière une couverture en espérant que tout se passe bien. L'un des rares jeux de stratégie qui récompense autant la prudence que la prise de risque, un bon joueur doit trouver l'équilibre parfait entre les deux. Entre la planification et la gestion d'imprévus.

L'ambiance générale est réussie. L'idée d'une humanité déjà vaincue qui tente de reprendre la planète à une occupation extraterrestre donne au jeu un ton plus désespéré que celui du premier XCOM. On n'est pas à la tête d'une organisation toute-puissante; on dirige une résistance qui manque de tout et qui doit improviser en permanence.

En revanche, XCOM 2 a aussi hérité de certains défauts qui font partie de son ADN. Le plus célèbre reste évidemment la précision. Voir un tir à 95 % rater au pire moment possible est une expérience que tous les joueurs de XCOM connaissent. Je comprends ce que les développeurs cherchaient à accomplir avec cette part d'aléatoire, mais il y a des moments où le jeu donne vraiment l'impression de se moquer de vous. Jouer en Iron Man c'est être sur de perdre des unités bêtement par la RNG.

Les missions chronométrées divisent également. Personnellement, je comprends leur utilité puisqu'elles empêchent les stratégies trop passives, mais certaines donnent davantage le sentiment de courir contre le compteur que de réfléchir tactiquement.

L'intelligence artificielle peut aussi produire des situations étranges. Il arrive que certains ennemis prennent des décisions absurdes ou qu'un événement imprévu transforme complètement une mission de manière peu crédible. Heureusement, ces cas restent relativement rares au regard du nombre d'heures que le jeu peut offrir et l'IA reste globalement maline.

Ce qui me fait revenir régulièrement sur XCOM 2, c'est surtout sa rejouabilité. Entre les différentes difficultés, les classes de soldats, les campagnes qui ne se ressemblent jamais vraiment et l'énorme scène de mods, il y a toujours une nouvelle histoire à raconter.

XCOM 2 n'est pas toujours juste. Il n'est pas toujours équilibré. Il peut parfois être brutal au point d'en devenir agaçant. Mais c'est justement parce qu'il accepte de laisser une place au chaos et à l'échec que chaque victoire paraît méritée.
Un jeu capable de vous faire détester la probabilité tout en vous donnant envie de relancer une campagne immédiatement après un échec mérite largement sa réputation.

Do I like the game? Yes, mostly... but there are too many issues for me to recommend this game (blame Steam for the pass/fail review structure)

PROS
- The combat is VERY enjoyable when it works (remember this "when it works" bit for later). As I said, I do in fact really like this game when it works.
- The diversity of the classes feels good
- The customizability of each soldier is quite nice (both functionally through abilities and gear, as well as free reign on a large range of cosmetic changes)
- The War of the Chosen DLC fixes quite a few issues and adds some fun things

CONS
- I normally NEVER save scum in games since I am willing to deal with my bad choices. This game, however, is designed very poorly in many ways that -- in my opinion -- forces you to save scum LIBERALLY just to not lose your entire team. I didn't keep track of how many times I save scummed in this game, but it was easily in the hundreds... I will say, however, that the game does allow very good save scumming, which is the only saving grace for the following issues I had.
    The reasoning for this? It has multiple factors:
    - The UI constantly gets in the way. Namely, you will move when you didn't mean to. You will shoot or activate an ability that you didn't mean to. You won't be able to see or hit the things you wanted to when you end your movement. You will run into unseen enemies mid-fight on accident and turn an easy fight into an unwinnable one... Just to name a few...
    - The way that enemy patrols are revealed is aggravating. It can easily turn a reasonable encounter into instant death if you move a single square in the wrong direction. This mechanic is rarely fun, and will often cause you to save scum when you get into the groove and forget that this awful mechanic will ruin your day, when you accidentally trip 1-2 more patrols...
    - Glitches are pretty common. Trying to place an ability and it will freak out and place it in a bad place. Pixel hunting is common and if you get it wrong because the camera bobbed just slightly for atmospheric effect... you got it, save scum.
    - Experimenting. This is actually kind of a positive, although if the UI was better then this wouldn't be necessary. My usual way of experimenting was 1-save, 2-experiment, 3-load save
- The UI... Oh the UI. It feels like graphic artists were fully in charge of the UI without any UX oversight. It is very pretty, and VERY aggravating. This game obviously chose form over function.
    - Animations are EVERYWHERE. Pretty? Sure, but you will be waiting just to go from one screen to the next because your camera has to take the time to pan across your entire base just to switch between 2 screens. Unskippable animations are everywhere, and even though they don't take very long, they get tiresome very quickly. In combat you will constantly be watching your soldiers doing the same stuff over and over, and sometimes it will suck you into a close-up animation that often clips behind a wall so you can't see what is happening anyway...
    - The UX is just... lackluster. I was constantly clicking in and out of menus with all of the stuff I wanted to view always at least 2 menu switching away in the best scenario and normally requiring somewhere around 6, especially when trying to gear up my soldiers for the current excursion. Some things were nice, but it was often a large hassle to get to what you want.
    - I don't know if it was my widescreen monitor, but there were often times that clicking on a valid location wouldn't register anything, so I had to pan around until the UI decided I had my screen in a position that it accepted.
    - Rotating the camera angle by 90 degrees is somewhat fine, but I found myself often moving the camera into a very weird spot just to see if a move location would line up for an ability, shot, or overwatch lanes. At least give the option to rotate by 45 degrees to line up the grid when needed...
- Enemy patrol reveals. This is an intentional design decision by the devs, and while some people might like it, I found it very aggravating. Essentially it boils down to this:
    option a) You ambush the patrol well -> you can easily mop up the group
    option b) The patrol wanders into your line of sight on THEIR TURN -> they get into position, but you have a chance to strike first. It usually goes fine and you can usually do a lot of damage before they get their turn.
    option c) You run into the patrol on YOUR TURN -> they react immediately, getting into positions advantageous for them. As soon as your turn ends they will all go. In my experience this happens all too easily, even when you know where the patrol is. One square that randomly sees through 2 windows and spies a single person of the patrol will trigger them. So often this happens on your last soldier's turn, which in turn allows the enemy patrol to walk all over your team, often critting and killing one or two of your soldiers before you can react. If you aren't concealed (and sometimes even if you are), there is NO INDICATION of when this will happen, and you are essentially ambushed.
    *NOTE*: The Reaper faction in the War of the Chosen makes this MUCH better, but it is still a game design that I do not like in general. There are other scouting abilities, but they feel terrible to use for the most part.
- The Alien Hunters DLC: As others have stated, these guys just feel terrible to fight. Randomly jumping into your encounters without any warning (listed as an easy encounter? Cool, bring your weaklings to train them up. Run into a game-ending boss in the middle of the encounter... feels real bad). Then, you give these random bosses an action after every one of your team's actions, means they could very well take 6 turns just from your team moving once each. It is awful... At least they give you very powerful armors in the end, but the design doesn't feel good to fight.
- Too random: I understand this is core to XCOM and many people love it, but I hate the random nature of combat. From missing a shot that has 98% chance to hit and has 75% chance to crit, all the way to a random mob hitting a huge crit across the map when you are behind full cover... It's frustrating and I hate it... At least you can eventually give all of your soldiers upgrades to move these percentages to 100%+ on most occasions, which is nice. But it's a game design I don't think is enjoyable.
- Disc Space Usage: This one was surprising, but with all of the saves, posters, soldier mugshots, etc, this game ended up chewing through 2GB+ of extra disc space (and put it in a place tracked by OneDrive, which quickly filled up my free version). Just a warning, this game saves a LOT of stuff to your disc.


tl;dr- I do actually enjoy the game if you go into it knowing that you will save scum VERY OFTEN. With that mindset it really isn't too bad overall.

What I love:

Concealment: Because you are a guerilla force, most missions start with your squad in "Concealment." The aliens don't know you're there yet. This allows you to set up devastating overwatches and coordinate spectacular ambushes to wipe out the first enemy pod before they can even react.

Mission Timers: XCOM 2 forces you to move. In the previous game, optimal play often meant slowly inching forward on overwatch. Here, almost every mission has a strict turn timer. It forces you to take calculated risks, pushing forward when you'd rather play it safe. It is stressful, but it generates incredible, cinematic moments of last-second escapes.

Enemy Variety: The ADVENT forces and their alien overlords are incredibly well-designed. From the mind-controlling Sectoids to the armor-shredding Mutons and the horrifying, shapeshifting Faceless, every enemy demands a different tactical response.

Overall: 7/10

This review is for the base game which I played 1st, before doing a run of War of the Chosen. This was a very good game overall and a different experience than most games I play :) I played XCOM 1 a few years ago and honestly didn't remember it being amazing or super fun, which is why I avoided playing XCOM 2 that I bought together with XCOM 1 for a few years. But XCOM 2 surprised me with how much fun I had with it :) I was going to give the game an 8/10 for the 1st half of the game, but the gameplay became a bit repetitive for the 2nd half and the enemy variety stagnated especially in the last 1/4 of the game. But still the game was pretty consistently fun and hilarious at times with the missed shots and domination of enemies with psi soldiers :P

I save-scummed because I had more fun with the game like that, rather than beating my head against the wall reloading a mission from the start if a soldier died. I only reloaded if a soldier was going to die or be wounded when almost all my other soldiers were wounded already. I didn't need to do so that many times but it definitely helped me enjoy the game more than if I didn't. I don't care what others think haha :D

The atmosphere and music were good, but I think I agree with others that the atmosphere/enemy design in the 1st game was better and more horror/creepy. But the gameplay was more varied & solid in the 2nd game, which is what I care about more, so I enjoyed the 2nd game overall more.

The story was compelling enough to keep me interested and I appreciate the variety of stories in the base game to keep the game fresh. I liked the Dr. Vahlen and Shen's father stories, as well as the little dialogue while on the ship from Central, Dr. Tygan, and Shen. The game did a good enough job to make me care and feel like this was a real conflict, so cudos to the writers. The story could be more fleshed out and stronger, with maybe more journal entries or dialogue giving background to the conflict. But it was enough for me to hear these interactions and read the research notes giving backstory :)

There was unfortunately a lack of polish in some aspects of the game, like the voiceover for Central during a few mission briefings not matching the subtitles and a few other dialogue like that throughout the game from Dr. Tygan and Shen. Also the "Make Items Available" buttons when editing your soldier loadouts never worked for me and just randomly seemed to remove 1 or 2 items from some soldiers. I had to go through all my "Available" or wounded soldiers to manually remove their items to equip to my squad, which became pretty annoying near the end especially when my squad was fairly customized with their items.

I also tried playing through the game again through the "expansion" War of the Chosen, which altered a lot of the game's mechanics more than added new content on top of the base game. I played through I think the first 5-6 missions, to the point when I had the first Retaliation mission with the first Chosen. I found myself not that interested to play through the game a 2nd time and found the War of the Chosen additions to be a little too much for me to care to manage. The story of the Chosen seemed more like a Saturday morning cartoon set of villains, who weren't established enough for me to have an interesting backstory for me to care to play the game again to discover it seems like their story/gameplay interactions as well as the 3 Factions' stories. The Factions were a little more interesting but not enough for me, with the most interesting being the ADVENT deserters. But yeah, overall I enjoyed the game but I think starting a new playthrough made me realize this was a 7/10 and not an 8/10 game, as I wasn't eager or open to replay the game which I find myself feeling with a number of 8/10 games I rate. Especially since this isn't the longest game, like 30-50 hours for me, it wouldn't be crazy to replay it compared to a Final Fantasy or long RPG, so I think sitting with my feelings about the game helped me realize I didn't enjoy it as much as I initially thought.

Overall a very good game but not as amazing as a lot of people say, at least for me. I think I don't love TRPG's enough to seek out more, but I would open to playing more that fit a setting or story that I am interested in, such as XCOM.

作为诞生于大型科幻架构游戏余晖时期的《XCOM2》，此时好兄弟《质量效应》《命令与征服》《死亡空间》等这些同样拥有大型且完整世界观设定的科幻游戏早已坟堆种树了，《XCOM2》无疑扛起了大旗，事实上它确实做到了。虽然从主线剧情来看XCOM2有点短小，但系列设定和内容表现上它是完整的。

XCOM 2 foi pra mim uma experiência complexa. Primeiramente eu consegui compreender porque ele é tão memorável pra tantas pessoas e até hoje é um dos jogos de estratégia e turno mais jogados na steam, com uma comunidade gigante.

Coisas que me marcaram: O design dos posters e as propagandas entre as missões são MUITO legais. Adorei a proposta que você não tá só lutando contra um governo, mas tentando arregimentar pessoas para sua causa. Apesar de ser meio nas coxas me recorda toda a proposta do starcraft wings of liberty(que provavelmente se inspirou em xcom também). Também acho muito mais interessante a ideia de lutar contra um governo totalitarista do que a propaganda pro "vigie sempre" e quase pseudo pro guerra de xcom 1. O sistema de classes é bem legal também.

Por outro lado, ter jogado vários jogos que bebem de XCOM 2 prejudicou em muito meu aproveitamento. O sistema "rígido" de não poder se mexer após atirar, a falta de clareza em alguns momentos sobre ações que encerram ou não seu turno, o RNG intenso, a progressão lenta em comparação a outros jogos foram acumulando frustração pra mim.

É legal pra construir uma lore em torno dos soldados - tem gente que coloca amigos e conhecidos pra se foderem pros aliens - e se você tiver disposição pra investir à fundo no jogo. Com DLC ele é bem longo, e é o tipo de jogo que se torna incrível quando vc mergulha pra compreender as minúcias de suas mecânicas. Mas se o lance é jogar de forma casual é uma boa se preparar pras frustrações e jogar com camolila.

A legendary 10-year masterclass in tactical stress, "95% hit chances," and pure heartbreak.

It’s 2026, and XCOM 2 is officially ten years old, yet it remains the gold standard against which every other turn-based tactics game is measured. Firaxis took the "underdog" fantasy and dialed it to eleven, turning you from a global superpower into a ragtag resistance movement operating out of a stolen alien ship. The gameplay is a perfect, agonizing loop of high-stakes decision-making. Every time you send your squad into the field, you aren't just playing a game; you’re managing a group of people you’ve grown to love, knowing full well that a single bad roll or a poorly timed "Sectopod" reveal can result in permanent death. It is brutal, it is unfair, and it is arguably the most satisfying strategy experience ever put on Steam.

The "War of the Chosen" expansion is no longer just DLC; in 2026, it’s considered the only way to truly experience the game. The addition of the Chosen—mini-bosses who taunt you, kidnap your soldiers, and sabotage your research—adds a layer of personal rivalry that was missing from the base game. When you combine that with the three new resistance factions and the "Sitrep" mission modifiers, no two campaigns ever feel the same. This is a game where you spend half your time in the "Avenger" base management screen, sweating over which research project to prioritize, and the other half in the field, screaming at your monitor because your best Ranger missed a point-blank shotgun blast. It is a masterpiece of "calculated risk" that rewards brilliance and punishes overconfidence with equal enthusiasm.

What truly keeps XCOM 2 alive a decade later is the sheer insanity of its modding community. With the "Long War of the Chosen" mod and thousands of custom voice packs, maps, and classes, you can essentially play this game forever. Whether you’re turning your soldiers into characters from Star Wars or adding 500+ mods to create a "Season 10" hardcore campaign like the top YouTubers, the flexibility of the engine is legendary. While the industry has moved on to newer titles, most strategy fans eventually find themselves crawling back to the Avenger. It’s a game that respects your intelligence, tests your patience, and provides a sense of triumph that few other titles can match. Good luck out there, Commander—the Council is watching.

XCOM 2 is a game that I wanted to like. I knew what I was getting into when I decided to play this game, because after having 100%'d Enemy Unknown, I understood XCOM's propensity for unfairness and player hostility. XCOM 2 was far worse than I had expected on that front, and I think it not only fails to learn the first game's lessons, but it continues to double-down on them - creating a game that both suffers and is worse because of it.

I'll start with what I liked. Visually, the game is absolutely an upgrade over the original - every enemy, model and texture seems at least a little better than the first game. Maps are more varied and complex, psionic abilities are more diverse and interesting, and there's a lot more in the customization department. Sound design is also excellently done - in terms of presentation, XCOM 2 is a far better game than it's predecessor - and conceptually, a lot of the ideas are solid, and lay a good foundation. The idea that the previous game was, at least in part, an alien-induced dream to use Earth's greatest tactical mind as their method of preventing and defeating rebellions? Inspired choice. Working in the shadows to build up from the ashes and re-take the world? Awesome! I was nodding along as i was seeing all this, expecting a tale of heroism, a bitter struggle against incrredible odds, and a final triumphant victory. I, sadly, was dissapointed.

XCOM 2 is a game that mistakes harrasing the player for tension. It's a game that gives you two options, and beats you over the head if you select the wrong one. Player agency is often removed and replaced with punishment and constant nagging unless you do things exactly how the game wants you to. Case in point - missions. Aside from the six story missions (including the final two at the end and the very first mission), the main bread and butter of the game is randomly arising events. The resistance might want help, or the council might ask you for something, a supply raid might be available, retribution might be being invoked against you by one of the chosen or something similar. These missions, while the bulk of the gameplay, are always offered as a choice - do you want to do them, or not? However, if you're just looking to pass the time, waiting on finishing a scan, or just wanting your soldiers to recover a smidge more before heading out? If you try to say no, the game will go "Seriously? Why are you doing that? No! Don't od that!", and if you continue to skip you're allowed to keep doing what you want to do... assuming that you don't try to start another scan or move around the map for any reason because then you'll be bombarded with the same "what are you doing, you're not supposed to actually skip these things" prompt. Continuing will result in you losing contact with the region, permanently losing income in that region even if you re-establish, losing any radar relays in that mission, and the council yelling at you. THis is every. single. optional. mission. The game "lets" you skip, but will harrass and belittle you if you actually do so. The worst part is, the punishment is often disproportional. If I skipped a Retrubution, that makes sense why i'd lose contact with the region, but a supply raid?? You're telling me that, because i'm good on loot, i decide to turn down the opportunity and the resistance just goes: "oh you don't want free stuff? i guess you hate us then" and just... dips. It's insane

Once you get in the missions, you are constantly harrassed with time-wasting quotes, locked cameras and constant, incessant hand-holding (with both tutorial and beginner VO off). I think i've spent about 10 hours in this game locked in place, unable to do anything because the game wants to show me the objective it already marked, or flavor text i've already heard a thousand times, or enemy information I ALREADY KNOW. For a game that wants to be replayed, it absolutely refuses to stop babying the player. Which is laughable,because the game doesn't actually hold your hand at all when it would matter. Want to know what a status is, or does? or how long it'll last? Screw you. Want to hear Bradford wax lyrical about trains? You got it!

the RNG system has somehow gotten worse. Line of sight bugs are far more common now, cover detection is even wonkier, and hit chance is laughably absurd. The amount of times my guy can miss at literal point blank, when the enemy hits and crits me every six attacks, is ludicrous. Want to know why you get crit so often? The Hit and crit roll is the same roll, which means that if your hit chance is lower than your crit chance and you hit, you will ALWAYS crit. Every. Single. Time. Which is why the AI crits so much more often - their hit chance is so low, that they're almost guaranteed to crit most times. This turns XCOM 2's main gameplay loop into a frustrating bum-rush simulator, where anything left to random chance (which is almost everything) will screw you at the drop of the hat, and you're just supposed to roll with it. In a good, well-designed strategy and tactics game, you should be able to do everything right and never lose - because, with the correct planning, knowledge and decision making - you will never make a mistake that the AI can punish. In XCOM 2, you can do everything right and still lose, or nothing right and still win, because damn near everything is filtered through an asinine and laughably punishing RNG system that creates unbelieveable and unreasonablely low hit rates.

The game has a stealth system, but often bugs out on the detection side, showing enemies detecting you when you were clearly out of their range for no reason. Enemies like the Codex are insanely opressive with little to no counterplay aside just immediately one-shotting them. The story is atrocious, insanely short, and never, ever stops being thrown at you. The Chosen (and the lost) serve as unreasonably painful obstacles early game, and free loot pinyata once you've gotten mag weapons. Balance is all over the place, and once I got even two months in, it was exceedingly rare for the game (on any of the difficulties) to put me in a place where i felt challenged, more than punished for doing the best with what I had. XCOM 2 shows the biggest flaws with it's difficulty that I've seen before - that being that, ultimately, the game is not difficult because it presents a logistical or mechanical challenge to the player, but because the game will just decide to kill your units. The deck is so stacked against you, that it stops being fun even to play your best cards. 

XCOM 2 took all the worst elements of EU and dialed them up to 11. Worse RNG, worse LOS, more bugs, worse enemies, and somehow worse balancing. Agency of the player is largely trimmed down and falsified, to the point where the game just might as well not allow you to skip missions whatsoever. I seriously wanted to have fun, and enjoy what XCOM 2 offers, but it gets to the point where it becomes clear the people behind this were horrendously rushed and bit off far more than they could chew. In the end, XCOM 2 is much like it's ending cutscene - left hanging on a forever unresolved plot point, the victim of haste and unresolved issues left hanging in the void. Just play EU.

XCOM 2 is honestly one of the most replayable strategy games I’ve played and easily one of my most played games with 350+ hours on it.

The gameplay loop is extremely satisfying. Building your squad, watching soldiers grow stronger over time, customizing their classes and loadouts, then risking everything in missions creates a really addictive cycle. The turn-based combat is tactical but also chill enough that you can play at your own pace, think through decisions, or even just casually play while doing something else on the side.

What makes the game nearly endless is the modding community. Mods completely transform the experience and can make every campaign feel different. From quality-of-life improvements to entirely new classes, enemies, mechanics, and progression systems, modding keeps the game fresh even after hundreds of hours.

One of the best recommendations is Long War 2 if you want a much longer and deeper campaign experience. It turns the game into a full-scale war simulator with more strategy, resource management, squad rotation, and overall complexity. If you enjoy RPG-style progression, slower pacing, and longer campaigns, it keeps the game spicy and highly replayable.

The downside is that the game can feel punishing, especially early on. Losing experienced soldiers hurts, mistakes snowball quickly, and RNG can sometimes make you question reality after missing a 95% shot. The learning curve is also much harder if you jump in blindly.

Overall, XCOM 2 is one of the best turn-based strategy games out there, especially if you enjoy tactical gameplay, progression systems, and games that can endlessly evolve through mods.

This is not for you if:

You dislike turn-based combat
You get frustrated easily with RNG or punishing gameplay
You prefer fast-paced action games
You don’t enjoy planning, positioning, and long-term squad management
You dislike repetitive gameplay loops or slower long-form progression

From earning my achievement for finishing the tutorial in 2017 to finally completing XCOM 2 in 2026, it has been quite a journey.

While I enjoyed the first game much more, there’s no doubt about how solid the XCOM 2 experience is. It’s one of those games that eventually goes on deep sale and, while it may be sitting in many people’s backlogs, it’s absolutely worth diving into. With only 30% of players completing the final mission, there are still many who have yet to experience everything the game has to offer.

It’s a game of patience and trial and error, where achieving victory brings guaranteed satisfaction. It will punish you if you take too long making decisions or if you fail to make them at all. You must constantly push new research and secure better weapons and armor, because the enemies will only grow stronger.

Its audio and soundtrack are fantastic, creating constant tension while maintaining a cinematic feel. The graphics still hold up very well and are beautifully presented. The maps are highly detailed, from the raindrops to the moving leaves, everything feels carefully crafted despite the isometric perspective.

This is not a game that really needs a review in 2026, but after finally finishing it, I felt it was worth mentioning once again for those still on the fence, or for those with the game sitting in their backlog thinking, “Today is the day I’ll finally start it.”

I’m not sure if we’ll ever get XCOM 3. The first game felt nearly perfect, while XCOM 2 made strategy both incredible and, at times, frustratingly limited due to the timed missions that force you to rush toward objectives whether you like it or not. XCOM: Chimera Squad was an interesting but very different take on the formula, so here’s hoping XCOM 3 happens one day. If it doesn’t, there are still plenty of hours of great gameplay to enjoy here.

This is one of the best turn-based strategy games I have ever played. It is also one of the hardest. The theme is very interesting. Earth has already lost the war. Aliens rule the world, and you lead a small resistance from a hidden base.
The difficulty is no joke. Every move counts. You will miss shots you thought were guaranteed hits. Your best soldiers can die forever because of one bad decision. Mission timers force you to take risks. The Avatar Project is always moving forward. The pressure never stops.
What I like about XCOM 2 is that you never know what will happen next. A simple task can turn into a disaster in two turns. 
TLDR; I would recommend the game to anyone who likes turn-based strategy games and doesn’t mind a steep learning curve.

Overall I liked the game, but felt more like an expansion to xcom 1 rather than a sequel. If you liked xcom 1, you'll probably like this game too.
Note that I only played the base game. I intend to replay the game again with the DLC at some point and will probably update this review if my opinion changes enough.

To get more into the specifics:
I liked a lot of the rebalancing from xcom 1. The secondary weapons are all very cool and fit each class well. The addition of the melee system was very cool. I liked the new specialist class a lot, hacking and remote healing are very cool additions. I like that psi is its own class now, rather than regular classes being able to use psi abilities. I like the armor system, I think it brings an interesting texture to battles. A lot of the new enemies were interesting, and the returning enemy redesigns all worked well.

However, there were a lot of things I also disliked. My biggest complaint is how buggy the game was. For example: units not attacking the enemy I indicated, and enemy pathing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ up and running around in circles. I also ran into a fun bug on the second to last level, where an enemy blew up my cover and the rubble blocked my unit from moving at all. Very cool. I also dislike how short the campaign is, my first run clocked in at about 30 hours on the dot (I don't remember if xcom 1 was this short as well). Tangentially; I was also fairly disappointed that there were only 2 weapon/armor tech upgrades, which were basically the same as xcom 1. Also the game ran surprisingly bad for a game from 2016. In the later levels especially lots of exploding cover and fire effects really tanked the game's performance, and I dipped all the way down to 30FPS at one point. My PC isn't top of the line or anything, but it should obliterate a game this old, and especially a strategy game which shouldn't need fancy fire graphics or physics simulations.
In general, I thought the game didn't evolve enough from xcom 1. You'll notice my list of likes are things that are slightly different than the systems in xcom 1. And most of my gripes were also present in xcom 1. I liked it more than I disliked it, but I'm not sure how much of that is this game's own merit, or if it's nostalgia for xcom 1.

XCOM 2 is simultaneously the most fun and the most frustrating game you will ever play. The developers created a great concept and then turned the game over to a bunch of degenerate gamblers who don't understand percentages to finish writing the code. You will miss so many 99% shots that you'll start to question if you know what 99% means. Reinforcements will drop in 5 feet from all of your units on overwatch and you will watch in disbelief as they fire so wildly, it's a miracle no one shot themselves. In fact, if one of your soldiers were to get depressed and decide to end it one night, it would take them multiple shots to finish the job. You will need your entire squad to kill one of their guys and they will one-shot you with a critical hit, even though you were across the map, up on a roof, hunkered down behind full cover, through 3 walls and a floor. What even is the point of cover if the enemy doesn't care if they live or die? They just run over and stand right beside you, going full kamikaze mode without a care in the world.

And you're going to need some mods, because for some reason the devs thought that strict timers in every mission was the best approach in a game about positioning and tactics. So if you don't want to be forced to be constantly moving forward during a gunfight, you'll need the mod to remove the timer. And if you don't want to waste several minutes hitting the same button for every squad member, you'll need mods for Extract All and Overwatch All. 

If save scumming was not a thing already, it would have been invented with this game. Every turn, something will happen that will make you go, "Wait. What?" and reload. If there is an XCOM 3, I'm begging the devs to rework the cover and percentage system. No one behind full cover should ever be critically hit. No one standing right next to a person should miss them. If you're going to force me to extract within a certain number of moves, don't have enemy attacks that are unavoidable and incapacitate my soldiers for 4+ turns. Don't have RNG hit chances that are clearly not RNG. I reloaded a 98% shot chance about 15 times and it missed every time. Which means the game has already decided beforehand if I'm going to hit or not.

XCOM 2 is a tactical turn-based RPG with additional strategy elements. It has incredible presentation, serviceable plot, an incredibly rich and deep gameplay, and tons of mods on top of that. I played it on Veteran with integrated DLCs and had no issues with any DLC content being too hard. 

One thing I must mention before the detailed review, however, is the technical state. The game leaves quite a lot to be desired: some actions leave the game "thinking" for 5-10 seconds before proceeding. In other cases, the game keeps "thinking" seemingly forever, while the sounds are still going on, so it's not a total freeze. Those endless "freezes" happened about 10 times, which is roughly each 5 hours, so not critical, but pretty annoying. 

DO NOT use Iron man in-game option, I don't think the game is stable enough for it.

Now, the details. Starting with presentation, it's very good. All the sounds are crisp and clear, and they don't get boring even after dozens of hours. Grenade explosions, rifle sounds, even basic unit quips are wonderfully implemented. Moreover, there is an option to diversify unit languages e.g. a German soldier would speak in German. I cannot vouch for accuracy, but it is a pretty neat feature. Alien language is appropriately alien and disturbing as well. 
The voice acting is also pretty good. As I mentioned, the plot is serviceable, so there isn't really any room for VAs to flex their muscles, but what we have is solid, no issues. 

Visually, the game looks pretty good for its age. I really enjoyed aliens' designs, many customisation options you have for your soldiers, and how the weapons/armour change as you upgrade them. 

The only thing I can complain about is a certain late-game alien. It looks extremely goofy and out of place, unfortunately. Doubly so because it has story relevance and is supposed to be very important for the narrative. I have zero idea why the devs thought its appearance would be appropriate for its role in the story. 

The gameplay is absolutely amazing. XCOM offers tons of options on both tactical and strategical levels, multiple different classes, and dozens of items. The game is punishing, but it feels largely fair (99% misses notwithstanding). Your missions can go right or wrong in hundreds of various ways, especially with Lost fighting against the aliens too.  I initially save scummed, but decided to only replay missions as I got better, and it made the experience more personal and engaging. I highly recommend embracing the RNG nature of the game and live with your mistakes; it's still very approachable and quite easy on Veteran. 

Strategic level is interesting too. It's not as action-packed as tactical battles, but it provides a very pleasant sense of progression and of slowly growing your network, pushing the aliens back bit by bit. Aliens, in their turn, fight back and make all sorts of issues for you. 

When it comes to the plot, there is nothing special nor surprising about it, but it doesn't detract from the experience whatsoever. The magic of XCOM, in my opinion, is not in the overarching plot, but in smaller stories and experiences you go through while playing. The actual narrative is just OK. 

To summarise, I highly recommend XCOM 2. Start with a lower difficulty and perhaps save scum initially to get a grasp of how the game works, then move to fewer saves. If you enjoy its gameplay loop, there is infinite replay potential with hundreds of mods, for instance LWOTC.

If you're on the fence about buying XCOM 2, ask yourself if you named your stuffed animals as a kid. If the answer is yes, you probably will like XCOM 2 regardless of the setting or gameplay. This is because XCOM 2 has a great framework for bringing any character you can think of to life. 

The following systems lead to a growing attachment to your soldiers:
- Customize name, race, sex, voice, language, nationality, outfit, backstory, disposition, color, patterns, and even create custom named weapons
- Out of mission consequences such as death, injury, mental trauma, loss of belongings, promotions, nicknames
- Randomized classes seem like a negative at first but allow for creative character and squad building. Make ninjas, drone operators, snipers, cowboys, heavy weapons guy, and more. 
- Cinematic camera/kill cam
- Soldiers can be seen interacting with each other/going about their days in your base
- Posters, photo mode, soldier bonds if you are play the War of the Chosen Expansion

In addition, Enemies feel unique in design and function, and combat in general always has this aspect of random chance which turns the combat into a game of strategic risk management, which leads to a lot of surprises, both good and bad.  

To conclude: Buy this game if you were the type of kid to have massive lego battles, and the setting at a first glance piques your interest. There's a lot of dlc, but my recommendation is to play the Vanilla game first, and with light, non-gameplay affecting mods at most. Then once you finish that and feel you'd like some more I'd definitely pick up WOTC. Maybe the bundle with Shen's last gift if you want robo soldiers.

i revisited the 2010 XCOM games and maybe i am simply not in a very forgiving mood, but i find them to be extremely aggravating and i am seriously failing to recall why i enjoyed them a decade ago. XCOM 2 maintains many things from XCOM EU that make the game slow and tedious, and manages to introduce new things that are slow and tedious in bizarre ways. while it is nice that certain actions no longer end your turn, like reloading or using certain tools, it is still often unclear whether something ends your turn or not, and the UI will move universal actions to a different order for each soldier, so i have to seriously look real hard at hotkey positions every time i use one lest i throw a grenade at my feet when i wanted to reload. managing your base is even more annoying as you must constantly move the Avenger to scan locations, and launching missions forces you to move to the region it is in. while i dont think any time is really passing during transit, i cannot begin to describe how much i hate the constant interruptions when scanning, and there is definitely a special mechanic to have missions appear when ~1 day is left on a scan. on higher difficulties i often found myself completely unable to get the monthly supply drop as multiple missions would force me away, and it is not explicitly stated how long a mission will be active before disappearing (though it is usually 1 day) so good luck trying to squeeze through a risky time crunch.

the fundamental experience involves lots of dice rolls, and your primary method of overcoming challenges is more akin to mitigating the effects of extenuating circumstances that are more or less outside of any direct control. what i find to be the most egregious aspect of XCOM EU and 2 is that the game is secretly cheating in your favor, and to me that makes it feel even more random, as i may be making what i assume to be advantageous tactical decisions, only succeeding because of a hidden stat boost, and later find myself in situations where an identical choice fails and i am left to wonder why.

finally, i strongly believe the developers are do not understand the differences in how the way their game works and how it is perceived to work. it has been said that they find it more exciting to have players forced to make bold and risky actions, and so thats why there are tight deadlines on missions and timed drops. what i would like to ask one of the developers, is if they are aware that your units cannot normally dash and shoot. i cannot count the number of times i have attempted to have a soldier dash to flank, reach an objective, or whatever, hoping they survive to their next turn, only to have them immediately killed, panicked, knocked out, etc. i also cannot count the number of times i have dashed everyone or moved to flank an enemy, and revealed an enemy squad. 

if you like turn-based tactics, you might like this recent XCOM series. as for me, i really cannot stomach the stylings of EU or 2 at the moment. some might disagree but i strongly prefer XCOM Chimera Squad. the randomness and tedium are substantially stripped away, and building your team is less like throwing infinite rookies into a grinder and seeing what happens.
