A kora ellenére még mai napig is kiváló stratégiai turn-base rendszerű játék. 90%-os leárazáson vettem meg a teljes DLC csomaggal együtt és annyit szerintem teljesen megért. Bízom benne, hogy lesz XCOM 3 is egyszer. 

POZITÍV

➤ Jó a sztori. 
Az első részben az emberiség kikapott. Itt a másodikban, egy gerilla felkelőcsapat vezető parancsnokaként fel kell szabadítanod az idegenek álltal uralt Föld bolygót. Rajtaütések, tudósok kiszabadítása börtönökből, felkelő bázisok elleni támadások visszaverése, gyárak és emberkísérleteket végző alien kutatólaborok elleni bombamerényletek,  stb stb. Minden akciót a játékos vezet a parancsnok személyében. Ezen felül van egy űrhajó szerű légibázis is, amin lehet építkezni, felszerelés és a katonákat fejleszten. A nyersanyagokkal takarékoskodni kell amik főleg az alien konvojok rajtaütéseiből és a felkelő bázisokról érkeznek amiket egymás után szabadtunk fel a bolygón mindenhol és kötünk össze rádión egymással, hogy megalakuljon az egységes ellenállás. 

➤ Sokat kell benne gondolkozni és taktikázni.
A körökre osztott harcnál nagyon fontos a fedezékhasználat, valamint az, hogy ki mire lát rá, mekkora területet tud fedezni, van e magaslati pont amiről jobban belátja a helyet, vagy éppen van e a közelében robbanásveszélyes anyag. Lehet sokat taktikázni ezzel és sokat gondolkodni, hogy mi lenne a legmegfelelőbb rajtaütési vagy éppen visszavonulási terv. 

Szerintem sokat ad a játékhoz, hogy katonák nem örök életűek, pont ugyanúgy meg tudnak halni mint NPC ellenfeleik és meg is fognak halni bármi komolyabb hibánál. Ezzel sokkal több súlyt helyezve a megfelelő tervezésre. 

Sajnos % arány van arra, hogy lesz e találat avagy nem és sajnos sokat mellé fognak lőni a katonák hacsak nincsen nekik mindenféle extra fejlesztés betéve és nem állnak előnyös helyen a map-on. Noha szerintem ez is csak segít abban, hogy a játékos jobban rá legyen kényszerítve a lehető legelőnyösebb fedezék és terephasználatra a harcok során. 

NEGATÍV

➤ Crash.
A töltőképernyő nem csak hosszú ideig tart de néha random crash-el közben az egész játék. 

➤ Idő után már repetitiív lesz. 
Egy idő után a játék vége felé a küldetések nagyon repetitívvé válnak amit csak az dob fel, hogy a játék random térképeket generál állandóan így legalább a terep más ha a feladatok nem is. Ellenségtípusból sincsen valami sok még az extra DLC tartalommal sem. De mire már unalmas lenne, kb ki is lehet játszani a játékot szerintem.

Игра пройдена неоднократно, в том числе на легенде + айронмене.
Вероятности - честные. На среднем и лёгком уровне сложности игра даже подыгрывает игроку, защищая от серии промахов и повышая средние шансы. На легенде нет никаких модификаторов для шансов. На 85% шанса выстрела в среднем надеяться не стоит, т.к. это означает, что примерно каждый шестой раз боец Вас обрадует промахом. Это математика такая же как и в жизни - если Вы бросаете кубик, и Вас устраивает любое число кроме 1, то не стоит удивляться если выпадет 1, просто нужно иметь запасной план на такой исход. 
Если усвоить эту банальную часть реальности, то игра становится кайфом, напряжённой, даже эпичной, но очень честной тактикой, в которую можно залипнуть на долгие часы. Ещё один ход, ещё одну миссию и спать - фираксисы умеют в такое.

1. По дефолту в игре очень скудные описания эффектов на поле боя, нет инфы ни о параметрах противников, ни о том что делает тот или иной скилл. Предполагается что всё нужно узнавать на опыте, но это даже по лору игры, где основной ресурс это "разведданные" - смотрится тупо. Т.е. с одной стороны при встрече с новым противником Брэдфорд или Тайган сразу рассказывают о том, что это за тварь и чего стоит опасаться, но посмотреть и почитать подробнее об этом просто негде, кроме как лезть на вики. Поэтому ставьте моды выводящие всю полезную информацию на экран, чтобы была, грубо говоря, нормальная кнопка "осмотреть" как у Ларианов в их играх. 
2. При смене языка игры, нельзя продолжить сейвы начатые на другом языке. Это вообще нонсенс. Правится модом. 
3. В случае с длс - не стоит ходить на сюжетные миссии типа "Последнего подарка Шень" сразу в тот момент, как они появляются, как бы Лили не нагнетала атмосферу о том, что нужно срочно бежать, спасать папочку. XCOM 2 ist für mich genau die Art von Spiel, die einen gleichzeitig begeistert und zur Weißglut treibt.
Die rundenbasierten Kämpfe sind richtig stark. Jede Mission fühlt sich wichtig an, und man überlegt oft länger an einem Zug, weil ein Fehler direkt Konsequenzen hat. Wenn ein Plan aufgeht, ist das unglaublich befriedigend – wenn nicht, schaut man dabei zu, wie alles langsam auseinanderfällt.

Was das Spiel für mich besonders macht, ist diese permanente Spannung. Man baut seine Truppe auf, gibt den Soldaten Namen, verbessert ihre Ausrüstung – und genau deshalb tut es auch weh, wenn jemand ausfällt. Dieses Risiko begleitet einen ständig und sorgt dafür, dass sich Siege wirklich verdient anfühlen.

Auch strategisch außerhalb der Missionen funktioniert das Spiel gut. Basis ausbauen, Forschung priorisieren, Einsätze auswählen – man hat immer das Gefühl, unter Druck Entscheidungen treffen zu müssen. Genau dieses „zu wenig Zeit für alles“ macht den Reiz aus.

Klar, manchmal kann der Zufallsfaktor frustrieren, und wenn ein Schuss daneben geht, obwohl er eigentlich sitzen sollte, fühlt sich das unfair an. Aber irgendwie gehört genau das auch dazu und macht die guten Momente umso stärker.

Für mich ist XCOM 2 ein intensives, forderndes und unglaublich motivierendes Taktikspiel, das einen immer wieder zurückholt – egal wie oft es einen gerade besiegt hat.

Against the Storm is one of the most addictive city builders I've played.

What makes it stand out is the roguelite structure. Instead of spending 20 hours building one perfect city, you're constantly starting new settlements, adapting to different resources, biomes, races and random events. Every run feels different, and there's always another reason to play "just one more."

The production chains and resource management are deep without becoming completely overwhelming, and the pressure from the storm gives the game a great sense of urgency. You're constantly making decisions about what to prioritize, what to sacrifice and how to keep your settlement alive.

The biggest downside is that if you're looking for a traditional city builder where you slowly build one beautiful, permanent city, this probably isn't for you. Settlements are temporary, and the game is much more focused on optimization and decision-making than decorating or creating a perfect city. Some runs can also feel a little repetitive once you've played for a long time.

But if you enjoy strategy, management games and roguelites, Against the Storm is an excellent combination of all three. It's polished, challenging, incredibly replayable and surprisingly easy to lose hours to.

I've been playing this game for a quite a while now and I must say: I really love this game.

It gets the best of a city builder and of a rogue-like game. You get to start a city from scratch and as soon as it gets well rounded and working, you leave it for the next one. So it never gets to the boring part where everything is already working and you just keep reproducing the winning formula.

The rogue-like features - different species, different building different bonuses (or cornersotnes, as they are called in this game), different scenarios and so on - make for very distinct cities. And the huge dificulty settings (24 possible levels) complement this variability quite nicely. The first nine levels are very friendly and let you get a feel for the game, and as soon as you think you got the hang of it, you can keep chalenging yourself as much as you want.

Besides that, the game really takes you into the world. The ever constant rain, the need to get all the suppllies as quickly as possible, the curiosity around the Queen (Who is her? Or maybe, what is her? How does she keep the storm out of the mountain? Why am I not allowed to see her?); all of it makes the game alive. The art and the music complement impecably, with lots of audio cues you learn without trying. How Pavlov would be proud of the thunder thirty seconds before the storm! You don't even notice it consciously, but you nevertheless start to make all the preparations required.

My only peeve with this game is that is it autosave only. You can never go back. I do understand what the devs were aiming for, but I don't feel that was really necessary. I believe a save mode on the world map would be a welcome feature. It would make the game much less stressful. But again, I do understand why there isn't. They want you to know that all your decisions are final. There is no return.

All in all, a very addictive game and a great work of art.

Calling this game a "city builder" can be a bit misleading so make sure you understand what you're getting into before hitting that "buy" button. The devs describe it as a "roguelite city builder" but that too can be confusing.

The game really is a chain of expeditions - or rather a sequence of chains. Each expedition has you pick a spot on the world map to embark at, yielding a number of modifiers that will apply to that expedition. Successful expeditions will yield certain rewards, some of which carry over or provide points for your tech tree, allowing you to unlock bonuses on all future expeditions. Prior expeditions also provide vantage points for new expeditions, allowing you to leap frog to new areas of the world map. After a certain number of expeditions the world map will be purged - save for some permanent changes you can make throughout - and require you to start a new chain of expeditions.

The expeditions are where the "city builder" aspect of the game lives. Resources are limited and the type of resources you can find vary expedition by expedition though eventually the biome and other modifiers can provide some clues. While you can unlock some buildings permanently in between expeditions, your options will mostly be limited by the choices you are presented with throughout the expedition, either by hitting certain milestones or fulfilling certain goals. The goals themselves unlock over time and usually provide you with two alternatives you can choose from. You won't be training specialized "units" and your population won't age or give birth, new settlers will be offered as rewards or as time passes and must be assigned to buildings to actually operate them.

It's probably more accurate to emphasize the "roguelite" aspect in "roguelite city builder" when it comes to the actual gameplay of the game. Instead of trying to follow a plan for building the perfect settlement it's usually best to adapt to how the expedition develops - most buildings have multiple purposes and (with some exceptions) there is usually more than one building serving each purpose so the challenge seems to lie in finding the right balance based on what resources are available and what you anticipate will become available as you unlock more of the expedition map by opening up "glens", sections that hold new resources or discoveries. Glens marked as dangerous will often provide larger rewards but also provide challenges requiring resources and time to address, often posing continous and irreversible harm until resolved (e.g. killing a portion of your population every few seconds or inflicting a debuff for the remainder of the expedition if the timer runs out).

The length of an expedition is ultimately determined by how quickly you can accumulate the necessary browny points by fulfilling goals - or how much you allow the "impatience" meter to fill up (which can usually be managed by simply fulfilling goals too). Meanwhile difficulty will increase as your population grows and your settlement expands into more and more sections of the map, resulting in increased "hostility" which will primarily affect your population's morale which in turn can mostly be managed by spending certain resources through certain buildings.

Don't buy this game if you are looking for something that will allow you to plan out a city or colony and see it grow and prosper over time. Every expedition will be fairly short-lived - either because you get lucky with the goals and finish early or because you fail to adapt (or misjudge the resources you'll discover) and run out of luck or decide to start over. You will likely make a lot of bad choices because it's often impossible to predict what will be the right one, if the right one was an option presented to you to begin with.

There are some production chains you need to keep in mind but nothing like the manufacturing madness of games like Factorio. The game juggles a large number of different resources but throughout a single expedition you will only ever deal with a small selection of them and they will always run out sooner rather than later. If many city builders seem to be geared towards a literally autistic level of detail and systemic complexity, this one is certainly more "ADHD-friendly". Also, because expeditions are mostly self-contained, (so far at least) there aren't really any major mistakes you can make that will ruin your playthrough - mistakes may quickly sink a given expedition but they won't linger and come back to haunt you several expeditions down the line.

All-in-all I would recommend this game, however. The expeditions can be chill or tense but always feel relatively short. This isn't one of those "just one more turn" forever-games but it can still suck you in for hours if you let it, while the gaps between expeditions still provide clean jump-off points if you'd rather do something else than spend your entire weekend in front of a screen. The default difficulty is challenging enough to not feel like a walk in the park outright without being punishingly cruel to casual players.

Against the Storm is a well made game with great ideas and I expect many people to enjoy it.

However, Against the Storm wasn't the game I was expecting.  I personally found the game to be more stressful than entertaining, and if you are like me then you might not enjoy it.

I was expecting more of an epic Everdell—building a cozy village in the middle of a dangerous wilderness.  I was expecting one of the increasingly popular mixes of "challenging yet chill", but there's not much chill here, and the wilderness dangers are mostly abstract.

The real danger is getting your supply chain gummed up.

I didn't expect Against the Storm to revolve so much around micromanagement.  From the videos I got the impression the management was a little higher level, and technically the game has all the higher level plumbing.  It almost feels like the designers took an automated game flow and went out of their way to interject busy work into it.

Pausing the game helps a lot, but at the end of the day it feels more like an RTS than a god game, even though it technically isn't an RTS.

I admire how the designers managed to fine tune the pacing of each expedition so circumstances look completely doomed until the 11th hour when suddenly everything pulls together and the objectives are achieved.  However, while I *admire* that as feat of design prowess, I don't actually *enjoy* it.

Also, for how polished and innovative the game is, the artwork is oddly bland.  It gets the job done, but it's not beautiful.  There again, I was expecting more Everdell.

In summary, Against the Storm does what it does very well, I just personally don't recommend it.

It took me a while to get around to reviewing this game, but as my >700 hours shows I can attest that it's a great game. 

This is a city builder with rougelike elements. You don't spend all your time building one city: instead you try to 'complete' settlements and then move on to the next one. There's incentive to winning as fast as possible because the campaign cycle has a limit to the number of in-game years that can pass.

Speaking of winning quickly, this game has strong optimization elements. Essentially you start with a small, primitive economy and gradually make it bigger and more advanced. You need to allocate your limited population appropriately, because overproduction of one resource is usually not as valuable as diversifying your economy. This aspect of the game is what makes playing it fun. Some other positive aspects I like are the seasons cycle, where each in-game year culminates in an epic Storm season where you need to be well prepared in order to lose population, and the soundtrack, which not coincidently has great Storm season music (and is great overall!) 

There's a few mechanics that I disliked that I'll mention briefly. First is how powerful Embarkation goods (basically bonus resources you start with) and the Trader (lets you trade resources at weak exchange rate) are. Both can be utilized to essentially jumpstart your economy from primitive to advanced very quickly. It feels very artificial, like you skipped some important steps of the game. Another aspect I was confused by was Impatience. This is a gauge that if it fills up you lose the game. So it should be a negative, but for some reason it reduces Hostility, which is a mechanic that basically makes your population less happy. Overall it's an addicting optimization city builder that can be played in bite-sized chunks because you constantly make new settlements. In late game difficulty you only get two of each every year, and whether your town survives often boils down to whether your first 5 blueprint picks had any synergy or not. Against the Storm is so good that the best thing I can say is how disappointed I was when I started to realize I was plateauing or couldn't find out anything new. I got a lot out of it, and wanted to play it constantly from the moment I started. It's so immersive, so cozy, but also challenging enough to require a lot of skill and focus. I loved everything about its roguelike elements that made each little venture different, and the game felt simply enormous to start out. Best of all, the UI is probably the BEST I've ever seen in a city simulator or any kind of strategy game. It easy to understand, to find new things, and to teach yourself. When I found out that DLC was available to expand my options, I instantly bought it after getting a taste of just the base game.

Set in a unique world that's all built around the concept of rainfall, you're tasked with exploring a procedurally generated wilderness with various terrains in the pursuit of completing a level they call a "seal." After doing so, you can play on these maps for longer and on higher difficulties before they rewrite themselves--all while steadily unlocking new buildings, races, and perks. As you learn the game, you're constantly finding new content in challenging events, the use of those optional perks, and given assignments to complete. Since you can pause and manipulate things as you like, it lets you be patient and make intelligent choices to protect your little settlements and ensure their survival. The graphics and artstyle look phenomenal, and the interesting technology and building options kept my interest for a long time. No two settlements are the same, and it encourages you to constantly try new ones (which is one of my favourite things, as compared to spending 20+ hours on one city). 

As the difficulty ramps up, you have more options but it can be severe. By the end of my interest, I was playing on Prestige 6 out of 20, and I just found that I was having so much trouble it had lost the relaxing vibes and I was starting to feel a little pigeon-holed into "metagaming" it, rather than using my creativity. That isn't to say someone else couldn't find a good blend of both, but I think this is one of the best games where you just free-form play, and don't focus as much on trying to meet the "point" of Seals. I just wish there was more ways to keep me engaged and having fun on those lower difficulties where I was able to engage my imagination, without having to feel the enormous struggle on the prestige difficulties. It's one of those games I would love to be able to erase my memory of, and try again. Especially as permanent upgrades are most interesting near the start, but it can take so long to finish the "tech-tree" that by the end, it feels like you aren't unlocking anything significant. 

This was one of my favourite games of the year, and one of the best city-builders I've seen; I hope that one day I'll be in the spirit to return to it and renew that hope it inspired during my first week of nonstop play.

Yeah, just gonna go ahead and say that if you enjoy puzzles, but not brain-breaking puzzles. If you enjoy strategy and management, but not insanely granular strategy and management. If you enjoy roguelikes, but want a new spin on the genre. Against the Storm stands alone as a perfect example. 

The way the game is paced should not be overlooked. It will challenge you and introduce you to new mechanics in such an enjoyable way. You won't even realize you're learning. The game has 24 difficulty settings. With that amount of flexibility, you can truly play the game how you want, and increase the difficulty marginally with each settlement or storm cycle. It makes for a game loop that takes a while to get old.

Now the bread and butter: The actual gameplay is excellent. It is as deep or shallow as you want it to be depending on your difficulty and how many systems you want to engage in. The pull and push tension of the three seasons work PERFECTLY with the soundtrack. 

And my god. This game has a banger soundtrack. The composer Mikołaj Kurpios is TALENTED. His soundscape combined with the constant drizzle of rain reminds me of early mornings playing Skyrim on a rainy summer day. It is honestly 10/10. Not a single bad track in the OST.

Each colony is a quick (45min-1.5hr, self contained expedition into the wilderness where you will work on producing goods to keep morale up. When morale is up, word will be sent to the Queen and she will be more patient with you and your colony. If not, she will get more and more impatient at your failures. 

The world building, the aesthetics, the sound, the music, the art. This game is special. And hey! The devs just announced that for their next project they are expanding the world and building a survival game a la valheim. I've played a ton of survival games and personally, the atmosphere makes or break them for me. If the devs follow through, I expect their next project to be successful. Because this world is DRIPPING with atmosphere.

Против непогоды: когда градостроение становится искусством (и испытанием нервов)

Помню тот вечер: за окном моросил дождь, настроение было «ничего не хочу», и я просто листала подборки игр, не ожидая ничего особенного. Against the Storm мелькнула в рекомендациях — мрачная, с приглушёнными красками и какой‑то тревожной эстетикой. «Ну ладно, — подумала, — пусть будет фоном, пока пью чай». А в итоге чай остыл, а я всё смотрела, как первые поселенцы робко ставят палатки под надвигающейся бурей. В этом было что‑то завораживающее: не эпичное спасение мира, а тихое, упорное противостояние стихии. И я пропала.

Первое впечатление было сродни попаданию в чужую, но притягательную реальность. Тёмное фэнтези здесь не про пафосные битвы, а про выживание и хрупкость человеческих (и не только) усилий. Расы — лисы, ящеры, люди, гарпии — не просто «юниты», а носители разных ритмов и настроений: одни суетятся и хватаются за всё подряд, другие действуют размеренно, будто знают, что спешка лишь приближает крах. Эта разница в темпераменте сразу задаёт игре особый тон: поселение получается не безликой схемой, а живым, пусть и беспокойным, сообществом. Уже в первые полчаса я ловила себя на том, что переживаю за этих крошечных фигурок, будто они настоящие.

Геймплей затягивает с первых минут. Строить города, балансировать ресурсы, следить за настроением жителей — в этом есть свой особый кайф. А элементы рогалика добавляют игре глубины: даже после провала ты не теряешь всё впустую — остаётся опыт и ресурсы для следующей попытки. Правда, после пятого подряд краха начала подозревать, что буря — это не просто погодное явление, а личный антагонист, который точно знает, где у меня самое уязвимое место.

Визуальная составляющая на высоте. Графика приятная, анимации плавные, а сам дизайн поселений даёт простор для творчества. Особенно круто выглядят бури — они по‑настоящему грозные. В такие моменты хочется просто сесть и смотреть, как стихия сметает труды нескольких часов… ну, или в панике достраивать ещё одну хижину в надежде, что «вот сейчас‑то точно всё будет хорошо».

Однако со временем стала заметна однообразность. После 20–30 часов игры некоторые механики начинают повторяться, а новые вызовы не всегда ощущаются как что‑то принципиально новое. Порой кажется, что развитие поселений идёт по заезженному сценарию: «построй склад, построй ещё один склад, построй третий склад, потому что ресурсы опять закончились». В какой‑то момент поймала себя на том, что мысленно напеваю: «Мы строили, строили и наконец построили… а потом пришла буря и всё сломала».

Вердикт: несмотря на некоторые недостатки, игра определённо стоит внимания. Она предлагает глубокий и увлекательный геймплей, красивую картинку и уникальную атмосферу. Если любите градостроительные симуляторы и готовы мириться с некоторой однообразностью — однозначно рекомендую попробовать.

Оценка: 8/10

I am really surprised by how much I'm enjoying this game. 

The obvious fear is it’s just a sandbox game with no direction or timeline - it is ALL time line. This is one of those games where you can spend 5 hours playing a scenario for like 30 minutes of in game run time. Maybe that's not everyone's bag but if it is yours - this is for you. 

You are constantly pausing and unpausing the scenario - I didn't believe the other reviews but - they do a really good job of making it feel like the best start up portions of something like civilization or starcraft II. The ironic thing is that you're just going to finish a run and do it all again but you don't care because it's so engaging and different every time.

Here's a couple notes I had while playing the game about things I liked:
1. The User Interface is really good. So many games neglect it these days but - the information you want is almost always apparent and easy to find. It takes some time to learn (I'm 60 hours in  right now) and I'm definitely using the wiki for some more intricate parts but tracking resources and production trees is really easy.

2. There's a lot of skill involved. It succeeds like StarCraft in that there are SO MANY variables to consider at one time that you really feel like you're putting your own playstyle into the game. There are portions of the game that are locked in that are completed the same way every time but generally the reason you are there in the first place is because you made a unique decisioin somewhere earlier in the scenario that requires it.

Let me be clear upfront: this is not a bad game. It's just not the game I thought I was buying.
I'm a city-builder veteran — Anno, Cities: Skylines. My joy comes from the slow pride of watching a town I planned grow into a permanent metropolis. Against the Storm's gorgeous art and moody atmosphere pulled me in instantly. But thirty hours in, I've reached a conclusion: this is a roguelite wearing a city builder's skin.
Every run follows the same script: chop wood, open glades, fill orders, survive the storm — and then, win or lose, your city is gone. The finest moment in any builder is when the supply chain finally clicks, the town takes shape, and you start dreaming about what comes next. Against the Storm picks exactly that moment to take it all away. Next run? Back to planks and firewood. There's a running joke that players don't even bother with screenshots — why capture something that vanishes in ninety minutes? And yes, the Citadel's permanent upgrades tick upward in the background, but a few percentage points of production speed is no substitute for the feeling that my city is still standing.
What frustrates me even more is how thoroughly randomness tramples planning. The joy loop of a city builder is plan → execute → reap. Here, it's draw → improvise → accept. Blueprints arrive as random three-way picks, fertile soil is scattered at random, traders haul random stock. One run hands you a farm blueprint on a map with no fertile soil; the next, you commit to a trade economy and the merchants stock nothing but junk. You're not planning a city — you're working for the RNG. Long-term strategy simply doesn't exist here; forest events and bad blueprint draws will shred a carefully laid route without apology. For a genre built on planning, that feels fundamentally wrong.
I can see why roguelike fans adore this loop: fast cycles, constant adaptation, climbing the Prestige ladder. The production values are genuinely high, and this review isn't written for them. It's for players who love city builders for accumulation and permanence. There are no cities here, only wave after wave of disposable settlements. No legacy, only resets. I don't want a hundred fresh starts. I want one city I can call my own.
Not recommended — not because it's bad, but because it takes away the very thing city-builder players treasure most: the sense of belonging that only time can build. This game hands you sandcastles, and the tide always wins.

The game can be highly recommended for what it does by design.
Its literally a rogue-like city builder where every time you build a town, you have different conditions and resources with a lot of options to customize your loadout and progression and gaining control over how your city develops.

The second major design point is that its essentially an EXTRACTION game. You build a base, you finish it up and when you do, you gain resources that you use to upgrade the main city unlocking meta upgrades and new stuff.

The third design point thats unique is that you can go prestige and add challenge beyond despair.
You can not only pick tough spots to settle on the world map, you can also pick spots with additional conditional effects (POIs), you can increase difficulty level by hand (which adds more conditions and debuffs) and then you can also do other things that increase difficulty.


This pretty much adds a ton of ways to play the game and focus on different strategies.
Theres lots of products to take care of, a lot of interactions between buildings and a lot to do.
I found myself fastforwarding, but only in the early stages in the lower branches of the tech tree.
And once you are going pro you can pretty much "NG+" the thing and whack yourself with tough challenges.

Admittedly my major negative point besides the somewhat cluttered effect salad going on, is the lack of coop.
This game could be even more incredible if there was a way to cooperate with a friend. Must not even be playing on the same map but maybe the same map but separate areas and interaction focusses on exchange, trade and doing expeditions together, maybe dealing with exploration together possibly with the option to connect your towns together if you really try to.

Maybe also progressing the main city together with your rewards or even having two separate main city to progress individually.

Hopefully a second game in this franchise features a coop mode.

If you're someone who just can't get enough of building self-sufficient settlements that survive against the odds in games like Stronghold and Frostpunk but you've already mined their campaigns for all they're worth, then Against the Storm will satisfy your cravings with nigh infinite replayability and depth through its roguelite structure!

I'm always a bit skeptical of roguelites as they can feel a bit shallow and repetitive at times compared to a more hand-crafted campaign, but I was surprised at how compelling the random factors you must adapt to, how campaign-like the overarching structure of going for seals was, and how deep the progression system was in constantly unlocking new mechanics that change the shape of the game in new ways, such as trade routes and the rainpunk system. Yes, there still is a certain level of repetition in building settlement after settlement, but for me, it's just got that certain je ne sais quoi I like in my roguelites where it doesn't just feel like some sort of slot machine.

I'm having a blast with the game, but it's not without its potential issues to look out for:

For one, as helpful as the tutorials and the interface can be...the game can still be rather overwhelming and confusing to grasp at first! I felt so confident going into my first game after playing the tutorials, only for it to feel like a nightmare trying to keep track of all the resource dependencies as well as the indecipherable menus with their endless array of buttons and doodads: it got to the point where I scrapped my settlement out of shame and restarted! I was almost scared off, but with a few more rounds of practice, I soon got into the groove, recognized the interface for what it was and appreciated just how much control and quality-of-life features there were at my fingertips, and just how much the game allows you to adapt out of (almost) any situation.

The other thing is that the game is a TIME VAMPIRE. I thought this was going to be a snacky experience since it was a roguelite, but no, each settlement can take up to around two hours to complete, and you've got around 4 settlements to do per run, in a game that wants multiple runs from you: that adds up to a lot! And this is even when I started to get proficient with the game and running it at 3x speed! Maybe I'm just bad or that doesn't sound like much to some people, but there were times where I felt like my soul was being sucked away as I played, unable to pry myself away until the settlement was complete...and realize I've missed all of my real-life responsibilities I had planned to do. Where did the time go? It's both a compliment and a warning at how addictive this game can be! Heck, I even started to get stressed out from constantly running simulations in my head even when I was away from the game!

TL;DR: Not the right fit for me, hope it's a better fit for you. Wanted to love it, but the game felt like a never-ending chore list with increasing management decisions and complexity that detracted from the fun instead of adding to the sense of adventure and accomplishment. I'm normally a person who LOVES this genre, but I honestly felt for being a game of the 2020s, it failed to meaningfully outdo games created in the 1990s and early 2000s (Age of Empires, Stronghold, Total War, ...I even liked SimAnt better).  Maybe the game was over-hyped, but the lack of depth in tutorials combined with the multifacted layers of complexity were not enjoyable. Could I complete tasks? Yes, but was it enjoyable? No. As someone who works in corporate management, this felt like a dreadful extension of my day job, from keeping villagers (employees) happy to analyzing bottlenecks and allocating resources. 

In short, if you're not yet a manager IRL and want to practice, Against the Storm might be fun. If you're looking for something enjoyable and you're already on the corporate ladder, this game will waste your time without a high ROI on enjoyment. Other titles that are much older had a higher fun factor for me.

Good luck, have fun, and take my subjective experience with a grain of salt! Can't return the game, but I might gift it on to an aspiring manager who wants to practice keeping digital beings happy while making them do work and managing production results. Again, this is way too close to my day job to be fun in any way...

At first i was kind of skeptical, but the whole game plays like a mix between a city builder and roguelike, every settlement is different, you have different races of villagers, different biomes, different effects, different buildings. Overall, brilliant idea, and brilliant execution. Would recommend to anyone that is into city builders / civ-like games or wants to try the genre.

先总结：这不是建造爽，这是资源分配规划的类肉鸽闯关游戏。

玩了四十多个小时了，上头是真的上头，但反过来思考，这个过程快乐吗，答案是并不，于是差评。总结下雷点：
1、生存建造类玩可直接忽视这个游戏，这个跟建造关系不大。虽然都有资源分配等等的相同点，但是游戏的胜利方式不同。这个游戏是声望够了就胜利，也就是说，你可以在居民都饿肚子城市快破产的情况下，通过清扫地图留下的任务，完成指示等方式获得声望点获得胜利，而且是达成的那一刻boom一下提醒你胜利了，毫无任何过场可言，太过策略导致经营的乐趣都没有了，再继续经营的话，一点奖励都没有，正反馈给的太差劲了。总之模拟经营类玩家，避着这款游戏总没错。
2、运气成分过大，声望升级获得的建筑是类肉鸽抽卡来选的，也就是说运气差的情况下，一个资源建筑都抽不出来，然后卡食物/衣服/满足导致卡关，眼睁睁看着失败。
3、平衡问题很大，游戏两大不平衡，一是每年给的赐福，强弱差距过大，比如每探索一个新森林给十个工具，能让你轻松做完危险森林的任务并滚雪球，很容易莫名其妙通关（回到上述问题1的奇妙状态），也可能刷新都刷完了，也只能拿到一些产量增加的buff，再一看，自己要不没采集点/采集点刷完了/跟小动物的需求不相关，然后这游戏又是一次循环好几个小关，想重开刷新？不存在的，第一个小关刷出来了，第二个小关你怎么办？重新开游戏吗？；二是各个建筑的原料需求巨特么离谱，比如你要造酒，最弱的线是造挖矿的（生产矿石），造木材，这俩合成木桶，再去整造酒的原料，最长合成路线需要五个建筑，但如果你有（赐福类）每生产10木材给3桶子，或者（其他建筑类），就可以2建筑合成酒，这合理吗？以此类推，存在大量的合成路线不平衡问题。我是玩运气还是玩策略？人不人狗不狗像什么？
4、合成路线的问题，逼人记路线。各个小动物的需求不一样，升级可选的建筑也不一样，而可选择的机会空间很小，一小关也就几次机会，一次也就三选一（cnm的你特么知道不知道种田玩家都是什么类型的搁这儿给我类肉鸽），导致的结果是，要强行分析观察和背诵，各个建筑的差异，怎么去选卡片能满足需求，同时对于一些朴实卡（比如锯木厂），还要尽可能的前期就造出来，不然中期就因为造居民建筑等等，卡木板卡到死。
5、局外养成，我测你么，不想多提了，nm40个小时才开12级的养成，而且加成远远没有运气重要。

写完这些之后，觉得吧给差评我还犹豫一下，还是太过中肯了，浪费了我这么多时间，只有上头，没有快乐，像是被偷走了两天人生。最后还是点题来一句，游戏设计师老冯飞上天了。

Apparently I have over 150 hours in this so I figure its about time I leave a review.

I will say first that my experience is not the technically intended one so take this as you will. I really enjoy the base gameplay, building little towns, exploring and branching out, then starting over with a new town is a lot of fun, but an important part of the gameplay is slowly increasing the difficulty as you go, and high difficulty and stress of it all just isn't something I enjoy. You can always continue to play on lower difficulties, but you won't be able to 100% the game, not even close (I got to maybe 1/3rd the way through). So if you prefer games to be more casual and not stressful than this probably isn't for you unless you will be happy only playing on the lower difficulty levels (and not a completionist like me lol).

If you are like me though and still want to play past that point, my own solution was modding. There is a console unlocker mod you can install which essentially lets you modify anything you want in-game, add any map modifier, any status/perk, give yourself items, etc. ie I can happily spend 60 in-game years deforesting the map to a truly ridiculous extent. Absolutely not the intended way to play and not for everyone but I feel I must mention it as its a key part of whats allowed me to continue to enjoy this game!

All that said, if you are interested in playing, mods or not, these are some thoughts from my experience, I'll be talking about it in terms of no mods being used as that obviously can considerably change the experience.

Gameplay;
- I haven't played any other game quite like this so its hard to compare, its a bit rougelike and townbuilder and resource management all at once. Early on it can have a more cozy feel but the stress will definitely be turned up as you progress through the difficulty levels.
- Expect it to be repetitive to some extent, there are a lot of changing variables like biome, villager types with different needs and specialties, which buildings you unlock, perks you get, etc. But the base town-building and end goal is the same every time. And of course in rougelike fashion you can upgrade your character to have additional permanent bonuses and unlocks as you progress.
- As there is an element of luck to which buildings, perks, resources, etc that you get, especially on later difficulties there is a lot of 'work with what you got', and its probably not going to be ideal, there is a lot of trying to juggle specific needs, finishing timed events that need specific items before they run out, etc. You'll need to micro-manage to some extent depending on the difficulty level, and the game will absolutely punish you for forgetting to handle something (obviously is way more chilled out on low difficulties though).
- Not all of the variables are completely randomized, particularly which biome each town is set in is chosen by you, as well as 1-2 of the villager species you start the town with. The overworld map also has map modifiers available in some areas that you can choose to use (or avoid). Its not fully customizable, but you have some control and ability to avoid things you dislike when starting a town.

Vibes;
- Immaculate, as long as you like rain.
- Jokes aside, this game is obviously intended to have a dreary tone, and its very consistent throughout. Not just visually either, the various events you encounter, even in the way the difficulty increases, etc, all adds to the worldbuilding and tone. Its never especially extreme or mean imo (and there are some bright spots), but do not go into this expecting a happy/uplifting game.
- I like all of the animal people :) The various species, buildings, biomes, etc are all visually distinct and beautiful, it has its own unique style to it that I find really nice to look at. I also like that the species feel unique to this world and not just a copy-paste from popular media (sorry but I'm tired of generic orcs/goblins/elves/etc).

DLC;
I've played a decent amount on base game before buying any DLC and sometimes they aren't worth it or feel like they should have been part of the base game, so I wanted to talk about it. I will only be talking about the frog DLC, I've not played on the bats yet. For context, the frog DLC adds 1 new species and 2 new biomes as well as some species/map specific perks, orders, etc. Both the new species and maps have their own quirks to them to mix up the gameplay when using them, as the other species and biome options do, but these have an extra level of difficulty to them (I'd say) compared to the base game. The Coastal Grove in particular I love to play on, but it really forces you to change up your normal gameplay. I would suggest playing on the base game first and if you like the randomization aspects and map modifies and want even more options you'll probably like this. They really feel like considerable thought and effort has been put into them to add some unique spins on the gameplay, but still feel like a logical extension of the game.


Overall even if the higher difficulties aren't for me, I can still really enjoy this even on the lower difficulties or with mods. A very solid game and its clear the devs have put a lot of thought and care into it, would certainly recommend giving it a try if it sounds up your alley at all!

Against the Storm (AtS) tries to differentiate itself by being a ‘cities’ builder rather than a traditional city builder. So whilst other games in the genre might focus on an epic campaign with one or a few cities, AtS has you building up many settlements as you progress through the campaign. This does mean it can get quite repetitive, having to start a new settlement from scratch each time. The exploration aspect also gets quite repetitive: clear trees, find new area, solve problems in that area, get rewards/punishment, and then repeat again. This is exacerbated by the fact that exploration is absolutely mandatory to progress, and you have to start your exploration from scratch as well every time you start a new settlement. The game’s extreme reliance on RNG can be a nuisance as well since it dictates far too many core aspects in each of your runs, from the race of the settlers you might get, to the blueprints that determine what you’re allowed to build, to what you’ll find in each new area, etc. The game’s narrative wants you to be ‘flexible’, but it becomes more of a frustration when you’re trying to patch up mistakes or problems you had in a previous settlement, only for your current settlement to not roll the blueprints/areas/resources/perks you need. Micromanagement and the user interface are problematic as well. For instance, you can choose which resources get consumed by each race. However, you have to set it up every time (because of the variation of settlers you might start with) with no way to lock it in or save it when you start your next settlement. There doesn’t seem to be hotkeys for constructing buildings as well, probably because, again, RNG plays a big factor in what buildings you’ll have access to.

I played AtS during the free weekend only, so this review reflects only what I was able to experience during that limited time. Sadly, the experience did not encourage me to continue playing the game further.

I usually like these kinds of games and though I don't exactly hate this game, it didn't scratch any itches.  The sound track is great, relaxing, and the sound of rain is a nice touch, that's about it for me. It felt like RNG had more of a say in if i was going to win or not. In the 3 games i played i felt like i was racing the clock to meet my objectives and then boom, it just ended. 2 of the times I didn't even notice i was close to winning my session, it just ended... Yipee? The game really boils down to a race against time and hoping you can get the right requirements (resources) at the right time to fulfill contracts.

There are a lot of different resources and structures that allow you to gather said resources, as well as structures to further craft the resources into more complex resources. The maps are randomly generated so which resources will be available to gather is inconsistent. This offers replay value, making every session feel a little different (this is a good thing). Overall i think think this works, but the UI isn't the best and it didn't really help me with the upkeep managing process. I would often over consume a resource, have idling workers waiting on resources to produce other resources, or build a structure for a resource node, only to have 2-3 of those nodes through my entire session. There are a decent amount of structures in this game but not all are available to you each play through. You will reach certain milestones that allow you to pick from 2-3 random blueprints of structures, so there is rng that you have navigate in hopes of winning. 

The queen will give you a choice of 2 random "Orders" to complete in order to get more blueprints. These contracts are random and will ask for things like "get X amount of resources", "Have 8 of a certain race type", "search X amount of nodes in the forest". You must complete these contracts in order to get enough points to win your current session. These contracts will somewhat dictate what buildings you need to gather resources to progress and fulfill them, but since the offered blueprints are random you will have to hope you get the right building in order to gather the right resource. On top of this you'll have to hope you find the right resource node and enough of it. Otherwise you'll be looking for other ways to obtain the needed resource, hoping those ways are available as well.

There is no combat and that's okay, but the mechanics of what i was doing felt repetitive. The flow was: Find resource, build structure to gather resource (if available), use resource to make other resource or structure to craft more resources. There were rarely moments where i was deciding on gathering one resource vs another. For the most part i wanted any and every resource that popped up. I'm sure at higher difficulties you have to be more decisive, but it wasn't like there was an abundance of resource nodes for me to decide between anyway. I also didn't feel that tackling a harder difficulty would be rewarding since it relies heavily on rng.

Good:
Music was solid and relaxing.
A decent amount of variables.
A cool progression system. 

Bad:
The UI isn't great.
Resource management wasn't fun for me. 
Too much rng for the variables and requirements and sometimes lacking in ways to get said requirments.

If you're thinking about buying this game, I urge you to "deep dive" as far as you can with some YT/"Let's Play", etc., so you can understand how shallow it is, before committing. I'm even more sad to have to come at this review so harshly, because these devs actually "tried something new". But the end result is: it just plain sucks.

Had a bit of fun on free weekend and figured the game would expose more layers of depth and fun, and that i'd find that level of insight and engagement that makes it really "click", but after playing it 30-40 more hours, I've learned it's truly just a colorful gui pasted on top of a very bland design. There's like 1/5th of an actual "real" game here. :( And that's after buying all the DLC. :( :( :(

Nothing at all to make it "pop", sadly.

Almost everything is pure abstraction. Doing well, doing poorly; winning, losing; finding or accomplishing something "surprising and cool", finding or accomplishing something "same old, same old"; even the most serious cases: "you're about to win", "you're about to lose" -- literally all is represented by numbers, and numbers alone. Like someone once said about the poor design of the firaxis Civ games: you just fill up a bunch of "buckets" (with numbers :P), simply to unlock new ways to fill the same buckets, or unlock new buckets which you also must fill with numbers. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ yawn.

Given the attempted technical depth, the UI/UX is an utter failure. There's simply not enough *guidance*. You won't want to keep your scan up 100% of the time, hovering over 40 different icons for tooltips, to try and even understand -- much less be able to effectively cope with -- the myriad effects on your settlement at any given point in time. And by the way, these effects change constantly. :(

There's a strategic meta-game which some people seem to find compelling but I'm not sure I'll ever get that far.

But since the base game is absolutely rife with "first time you encounter this, you will lose", mechanics, who the hell wants to strive for the meta-game?

(Well, I *will*, because I want the achievements. But I definitely won't enjoy the slog. Luckily it's easy to cheat at ... indeed the only regard in which this game is not a total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.)

Сразу хочется сказать, что игра вполне [b]неплохая[/b], атмосферка мира с постоянным дождём и оформление доставляют, и даже удовольствие от неё можно получать, но...

Игра заявлена как "Градостроительный симулятор с элементами рогалика". Моя проблема в том, что это наоборот, рогалик с элементами градостроилки. И если случайно генерирующийся уровень, к условиям которого надо подстроиться, у меня не вызывает каких-то проблем, и даже к таймеру я готов был привыкнуть, то вот вся якобы "сложность" возникает из-за того, что все задания, жителей и выдаваемые пачками здания на выбор игра может тебе нароллить так, что только за голову остаётся хвататься. Так, последний город для закрытия печати едва не был слит, ведь для двух заданий из трёх игра просто не заспавнила мне ресурсов и не выдала мне нужное производственное здание, а для третьего мне пришлось перерубить половину леса в поисках нужных ивентов, в процессе слив половину таймера и накопив враждебности леса. Боюсь представлять, что там на сложностях выше творится.

При этом от местной мета-прогрессии вообще не ощущается какого-то удовлетворения, ведь за один полный цикл (~6 часов и четыре города), за который я закрыл первую печать, я смог открыть буквально три-четыре бессмысленных апгрейда из серии "+2% к тому, что лесоруб сегодня зычно пёрнет", и в этом тонко размазанном потоке мусора надо вылавливать по всей ветке прокачки всякие QOL-апгрейды на возможность рероллить задания и прочее.

В общем, спасибо бесплатным выходным за то, что я смог опробовать игру, и может когда-нибудь я её куплю по скидке -90%, закрою на платину и переосмыслю этот обзор, но пока игра закинута в долгий ящик.

P.S. А ещё странно, что к игре выпустили уже два ДЛС, но разработчики так и не догадались сделать режим с отстройкой одного отдельного взятого города на огромном участке леса, на развитие которого тебе выдан один целый цикл (условно игровые 20-30 лет), с последующей эвакуацией под стены столицы при приближении Бури, а-ля Винтерхоум из Frostpunk с наградами и прочим. Pros:
It is a gorgeous game with excellent sound/music, and an interesting world. 
The gameplay feels/looks like Warcraft... without the war?
A pretty reasonably deep (but not overly complex) upgrade system
the controls and tools are top-notch, making gameplay intuitive and easy to pick up.

Cons:
The game is fundamentally flawed - at its core, because of the fact that it combines an overall vibe of relaxing builder game concepts with a fundamentally more stressful, RNG-based roguelite system of building unlocks in each map. 
>>> In other words, the fact that you can feel "at the mercy" of the randomness of unlocks means that you may find it more difficult to get the more relaxing aspects of a relaxing builder-style game - while the more chill vibes of the game overall mean that people who like the RNG-heavy mechanics may feel bored with the gameplay over time. 

Because I can only offer thumbs up or thumbs down, after having played during a free-play week for several days, I can say that this game is an excellent effort at the impossible task of combining these ideas. But if you want a relaxing game, there are better options, if you want roguelite, there are better options. If you are somehow the person who wants to experience both? You will love this game!

★게임 방식: 총독이 되어 마을을 건설하고 주민을 관리하는 로그라이크 도시 건설 게임.

★기본 클리어 조건: '여왕의 노여움'이 가득 차기 전에 주민 만족도를 높이거나 퀘스트를 완료하여 '평판'을 끝까지 채우면 마을 1개 건설 완료.

★핵심 재미 요소:

1. 높은 리플레이성: 판당 30분 내외의 짧은 플레이 타임, 매판 무작위로 바뀌는 조건·지형·이벤트 덕분에 매번 새로운 도전의 재미를 제공함.

2. 넓은 세계관: 다회차 플레이를 통해 넓은 세계지도 곳곳에 여러 개의 마을을 계속해서 개척하고 건설해 나가야 함.

3. 긴장감 넘치는 시스템: 시간이 흐를수록 페널티를 주는 '여왕의 노여움'과 '숲의 적의' 수치가 쌓여 빠른 판단과 순발력이 필요함.

★심도 있는 전략 및 운영 요소:

- 생산 효율성 계산: 같은 물품(예: 판자)이라도 제재소, 목공소 등 건물에 따라 생산 효율(★ 등급)이 달라 상황에 맞는 최적의 건물을 고르는 재미가 있음.

- 제한적인 교역 시스템: 상인이 주기적으로 방문할 때나 특정 조건을 만족해야 물건을 사고팔 수 있으며, 이웃 마을과의 교역로 개설에도 인력과 자원이 소모되는 등 타이밍과 조건 관리가 필수적임.

- 다채로운 평판 관리: 종족별 맞춤형 요구품을 생산해 '주민 만족도'를 채우거나, 여왕의 '지시 퀘스트'를 해결하며 평판을 올리는 유기적인 시스템.

★로그라이크식 성장 요소:

- 성채 영구 업그레이드: 게임을 클리어하거나 실패하더라도 획득한 자원으로 기지(성채)를 영구적으로 업그레이드할 수 있음.

I was added this to my wishlist in 2023, and I was excited to play because I like roguelikes/roguelites and city builders. I appreciate the idea, but I just didn't like most of it.

First, this is micromanagement hell. You have to check which race goes where, what each workplace produces, and which raw materials it needs. Once a resource is depleted, you have to keep juggling recipes. Then you juggle workers, moving them from here to there. If you pause a workplace for whatever reason and start it again, you have to manually assign the workers all over again. Then you juggle buildings too, constantly moving them left and right.

You produce way too many things, but most of the time you don't know why. You can set production limits, but you don't know what you will need, when you will need it, or how much you will need. Will this event ask for planks? Will it ask for eggs? Should I stop my workers from eating eggs? How do I let them eat eggs while keeping exactly 12 in storage in case an event needs them? It's just too confusing.

Building parts are another annoyance. They're an artificial bottleneck that stops you from building what you actually need. Instead of expanding your settlement the way you want, you're constantly forced to demolish buildings just to recycle the parts and place something else. It doesn't add meaningful strategy; it just creates even more unnecessary micromanagement.

Then there are the building and perk unlocks. Multiple buildings do the same thing. One workplace produces A, B, and C, while another produces A, D, and F. Some buildings are simply larger or upgraded versions of existing ones, while others just overlap with what you already have. But when it comes to unlocks, it's micromanagement hell all over again. You have to check every building to see whether it can produce A or B; otherwise, you end up with three different buildings all collecting or producing the same resource. For example, five different buildings produce fabric, and six different buildings produce coats.

The perks aren't any better. They say things like "Increase X by +1," but you can't even produce or use that thing yet. Maybe you will unlock it later, maybe you won't. Every time you unlock something, you have to go through every perk and every building you've already unlocked just to figure out whether that perk is actually useful.

I played the two tutorial missions and one regular mission from the map in 5 hours. Every completed mission gives you upgrade currency that slowly adds tiny passive bonuses like "+2% villager speed" and similar stats.

The UI is crazy too. You even have to micromanage your stats in that UI. The game buries you under dozens of modifiers, bonuses, penalties, resolve thresholds, consumption preferences, corruption, hostility, impatience, reputation... you're constantly opening panels, switching tabs and mouse over on an icon to figure out why something suddenly changed. 

I'm overwhelmed.

I initially wrote a good review of this game until i realized how insanely annoying it is lol. I enjoyed some of it, but i've had many frustrations with it that make me not want to recommend it... I understand i have a lot of time in this game, but just be aware these frustrations were obvious early on, i had assumed playing for longer and getting used to it would make them less annoying... but it doesn't... And i had spent a lot of time playing it listening to podcasts and the sort, i would not have played it so long otherwise.

It's a pretty fun survival village builder, akin to Banished or Anno, albeit with a twist. Instead of playing one long settlement, you play many settlements, which should solve the rut i always run into in these types of games(that is, once you get too far in, managing your settlement becomes quite annoying, logistics is a pain) But, it only slightly remedies it, as logistics still do get annoying later on and you always end up with too many villagers and no way to turn away villagers when they come.

I do think the storm aspect and hearth is cool, it has a hearth kinda like frostpunk, you need to burn wood or coal or other resources to keep your people happy(though i don't really know exactly why lol, maybe it explains it somewhere but i never caught on to that)

The trade system is pretty cool, though it takes some learning, it's kinda cool how you can just send off resources for money 

Okay,here's the major annoyances this game has...
-Hostility, it goes up for stupid reasons, there's very few ways to bring it down permanently, it goes up over time, while discovering, completing events, getting new villagers... sorta discourages you from doing anything tbh.
-And to add to that, during the storm resolve ALWAYS drops like crazy, i don't know if this is by design but it's quite annoying. Hostility increases the severity of the storm. Sometimes even killing people. 
-Resolve is annoying to increase... It's basically morale, you increase it by fulfilling needs. Yet, you need to unlock a ton of blueprints every game to fulfill these needs, for example if you want a tavern, you need to unlock several blueprints, the tavern itself, something to "hold" the beer(barrels or pots), a farm, and something to produce beer. And if a species' resolve gets low, it basically gives a timer and one will leave every time the timer runs out. 
-Different species are just an added layer of frustration. Each different species has different needs, so when you finally get that tavern, oh, sorry, that only benefits the humans with you, you need something else for the harpies. 
-Tools. They're not always easy to produce, they're necessary for increasing reputation with crates you find, yet most games you just have to FIND them. Reputation is basically necessary for A. Unlocking new blueprints and B. winning the game
-The aforementioned crates need rocks or fossils(??) to open, if you want to get the resources inside instead of sending them for reputation. And what if you haven't found any stone or fossil deposits? Sorry, those crates cannot be opened until you do, so they sit there, mocking you! lol

I think this game would be much better if 
1. Necessary blueprints did not need to be unlocked every single game, why not just depend on actually finding the resources you need rather than unlocking blueprints?
2. Hostility needs a better way to be dealt with, there are SOME ways to lower it, and you can burn extra resources to temporarily lower it, but it goes back up again immediately when you run out. Hostility should go up over time, not every single move you make. 
3. Let you pick one species per game. I hate having to deal with multiple different needs in a game where even dealing with one need is a challenge already... OR keep it multiple species but have resolve affect work speed instead of making them leave. 

Though i don't expect the dev to overhaul these things just for my criticism.... I think pointing out these issues will help people to make an informed decision about this game. It's seriously a good concept, but... delivered very poorly.

I’d give Against the Storm a solid 9/10.

And just for context: besides my playtime shown on Steam, I also have around 65–70 additional hours in the game from when I played it through the Xbox App while it was still on Game Pass. 
What initially got me was the cozy vibe. There’s something strangely relaxing about building a settlement in an endlessly hostile forest while the storm is getting worse, three glade events are ticking down, and you’re desperately waiting for one trader to bring the exact thing that might save your run. What kept me playing, though, is how flexible the game is. Sometimes I want a relatively casual session where I just build a decent little settlement and chill. Other times I want to stare at production chains, optimize worker placement, juggle trade routes, calculate hostility thresholds, and completely reorganize my economy because I suddenly realized I can squeeze out the last two reputation points by making everyone cook meat for the harpies and lizards. And that is probably my favorite thing about Against the Storm: you do not need to build the perfect city. You need to build a city that is good enough to win. 
The gameplay loop works incredibly well. Everyone will naturally develop their own preferred playstyle, but the blueprint system, cornerstones, species combinations and available resources often gently force you to look outside your comfort zone. I am very much a glade-opening kind of player. I like having lots of workers, I am not particularly scared of hostility, and I will absolutely open another dangerous glade when common sense suggests that maybe I should calm down for five minutes. The risk/reward system around opening glades is top tier for me. 
The RNG is a big part of the experience, and most of the time I think the game handles it very well. Sometimes you really want a specific blueprint or cornerstone and simply do not get it. That can be annoying, but usually the interesting part is how you adapt. A bad random event can become a huge advantage if you react to it properly, and turning a seemingly terrible situation into a profitable one feels fantastic.
There is, however, one RNG-related issue that I would really like to see improved: tools. Sometimes I end up with three, four or five crates sitting in glades, but I have absolutely no access to tools. No trader sells them. No blueprint lets me produce them. Nothing. And unlike many other bad situations in Against the Storm, there is not always a meaningful strategic response here. You cannot outplay the problem if the game simply refuses to give you any possible route toward tools. I would love to see some kind of expensive emergency fallback option: inefficient production, a guaranteed but costly trader option, a special order, something. It should not be easy or cheap, but there should ideally be a way to react strategically instead of just accepting that those crates are now forest decoration.
The production chains themselves are not especially difficult to understand. Usually it is something like:
raw resource → intermediate material → finished product → possibly a service building
The complexity comes from scale. One finished product may require two or three other buildings, which themselves need materials from another two or three sources. At some point you look at your settlement and realize that half your population is involved in an industrial conspiracy to produce twelve coats. This is fun, but I do think the game could use more advanced production and logistics rules. For example, I would love to be able to set a condition like: “Only produce flour when stored grain is above 30.” There are many situations where rules like this would make optimization much more precise and reduce unnecessary micromanagement. For a game with such deep production systems, this feels like a natural area for further improvement.
I also think the hub upgrade system becomes less interesting over time. Early on, the bonuses feel meaningful. Later, upgrading hubs starts to feel more like a mandatory checklist where you spend resources and worker time placing decorations because that is simply the efficient thing to do. I would love to see more meaningful choices here, instead of hub upgrades becoming an automatic part of every settlement.
The metaprogression is generally satisfying, although personally I think unlocks could happen maybe 5–10% faster. Your actual player level can sometimes feel like it moves ahead of the things you are unlocking.
The UI and UX, however, are excellent, especially considering how much information the game has to communicate. There are still small things that could be improved, but the developers clearly continue working on this, including the most recent patches.
Visually, the game is fantastic. The art style is sharp, distinctive and full of personality, and the atmosphere is honestly one of the best parts of the whole experience. I cannot say the music particularly stuck with me (I genuinely had a moment where I thought, “Wait, is there music?”) but the overall mood absolutely works.
Against the Storm is at its best when you are completely immersed in the settlement. When you feel the importance of the next trade route in your bones. When you are deciding whether opening one more glade is genius or stupidity. When the storm is hitting hard, everything is barely holding together, and you are nervously waiting for it to end so damage control can begin. That is when the game really gets under your skin.
It can be cozy. It can be stressful. It can be a city builder, an optimization puzzle, a roguelite, or all three at once.

If you like City/Colony Builder sort of games, honestly stay away from this game. The mechanics of the game make it almost impossible to have fun that way. You basically have a meter, and once it goes all blue (your meter) or all red (enemy meter), the game is over. So you can't really chill and enjoy the good bits of it (the colony/city builder with neat randomized stories involved), because you always will have to put up with said meter. Doesn't help that you have a card meta game within it, and you're limited to three cards, with one decision, and you have orders (obligations) that help fill up the blue meter, AND you have to choose between two helpful items, AND you have to chose between two to three sets of new settlers. 

It doesn't give you time to rest and enjoy just building out the settlement. Honestly just wished they did away with most of it outside of obligations, stories, and help, and just give levels where you unlock buildings, until you have all of them. You can just keep the blue meter, and if that maxes out, you win (like Two Point does it), where you could continue it out or go to the next level. 

That's the other issue, you just get random buildings flung at you. So you never understand what the buildings exactly do, I end up most of the time building the wrong building because of this. Doesn't help that each map is themed. That wouldn't be a problem if you didn't have the red meter and constant needless stress of a game over. So building the wrong buildings for the map will end up with you losing really quickly, which gets really annoying. 

Honestly, just a confusing mess of a game. If you can "get" this game, or can wrap your head around it's confusing nature, I'm sure it could be fun and challenging. But honestly, this game doesn't do it for me.

I spent many hours trying to like this game now, and while it has some quailities, ultimately I can't. There are too many moving parts and constant time pressure. It seems, the game was designed to never give the player a sense of control. That's not for me. 

I'm talking about countless resources and production goods, many many building types, each of which offering a unique combination of 3 production "recipies", overlapping with other building types but sometimes in different efficiency grades, with many substitutable input resources. Then there's multiple population races, each with different specialization bonuses and many different demands (partly overlapping again). And on top of that there's countless bonuses, modifiers, events, and what not.

And if that weren't enough, you are [b]constantly[/b] forced to make decisions about random options you get -- and which you only have vague ideas about. Your next available building types, tasks, rewards, bonuses, population newcomers, solutions to events, upgrades, etc. This is before a mission, during a mission, and after the mission. They really push that decision making over the top.

Granted, this creates some excitement. During the game there's usually a new choice available before you even made up your mind about the previous choice. Once you're into it, this can get the dopamine cycle going. Hence, all the good reviews, I suppose. Also, it creates replayability.

But on the other side, it's only designed to play over and over again. You're cranking out settlements under time pressure, never with much planning or feeling of control, basically improvising with all the options thrown at you and just a rough idea of what you're doing. 

And once you somehow managed to score sufficient reputation points, it's all over. There's no time to optimize, beautify, extend or simply enjoy the settlement you just created. That's probably my main criticism. It's all just a rush to beat the timer. Plus, I personally don't like this constant dark and rainy mood. I'd prefer a happy medieval town with sunshine and birds singing. But ok, that's subjective.

I will express my respect to the development team, though. Keeping an overview about all the aforementioned elements of the game... hats off. Their diagrams must stretch across entire walls. Also, on the bright side, the game's hardware requirements are really fair. I think that speaks for good programming.

On the bottom line, if you get a kick from juggling complexity under time pressure, Against the Storm may be for you. If you want a more relaxed and strategic gameplay that allows planning, improving and enjoying your settlement a little longer, I don't recommend it. I'm gonna look for a more controllable game now, Banished maybe, Farthest Frontier, or HistoriCity. I did enjoy Townsmen a lot in recent years, but that's just mobile, I think.

I hope this helped. Peace and out.

7.10更新：仔细测试了一下，看来是我之前理解错了（游戏中的文本确实让人误解）。城市规划虽然削了，但没有削废，游戏内文本描述是“所有可居住房屋加起来最多16位”，但游戏内的实际效果，应该参考更新日志的内容，也就是“单栋房屋或庇护所的最大居住容量上限（来自辅助技能、升级与基石的加成）从 20 降至 16。”，我在游戏中测试了一下，结论来说，在拥有24栋可居住房屋的情况下，在点了基石“城市规划”并完成10条贸易路线之后，每一栋可居住房屋都增加了一个居住容量，换言之，并非“所有房屋总共加起来只有额外16个居住容量”，而是单个房屋吃满所有加成之后，最多有16个居住位。这个算是下调，但还不至于算是砍废了，之前言重了，改为好评以示歉意。不过仍然，这个改动并不受欢迎，如果之后真正出现了重大削弱，还是会改为差评。

———分割线———

游戏很不错，我也很喜欢，游戏时间显示只有不到两百小时，是因为我经常离线模式玩，如果算上离线时间，保守估计500小时起步。这里说明一下，我的玩法比较特殊，我并不注重每一局快速拿满声望的过程，而是享受在拿满声望之后，继续建设定居点的Endgame玩法，我往往会使用CE来强化游戏过程的稳定性（主要是刷基石和蓝图），尤其确保定居点有足够的可再生资源，从而可以搭配一些强大的基石来产生巨额产能，比如“香料”基石搭配雨水磨坊搭配饼干配方从而产生巨额的根茎、香草、饼干产能，然后搭配基石与配方，利用巨额根茎产能来获得巨额焚香，或利用巨额的香草产能来获得巨额的成包供给品。

总之，这个游戏给了我很多乐趣，从抢先发行时期一直玩到现在，建设繁盛的定居点是很有成就感的事情，整体来说我很喜欢，但这次我还是要给差评是因为，我发现制作组喜欢削东西，这种行为我实在难以认同。

今天刚更新一波到1.10.3R版本，刚进游戏就看到基石“城市规划”被彻底砍废了，这原本是我非常喜欢用的一个传奇基石。说真的，传奇基石中很多废物，和它们的名字“传奇基石”完全不符，很多时候不如史诗基石好用。城市规划是为数不多真正有强度的传奇基石，在Endgame中也是非常有用的。然后就看到它被砍了，甚至可以说，被砍废了。乃至甚至“拥挤的房子”这种本来就强度不高的基石也被砍了。

首先，这是个单机游戏，单机游戏应该是致力于服务玩家的游戏体验的，这不是PVP，也没有天梯榜。其次，这是个Roguelike游戏，是有随机性的，没有什么办法去稳定地获取这些基石，有时候重抽次数用完了，也只能拿到没什么用的基石。基石之间强度有参差，可以理解，Roguelike游戏嘛，玩家对不同基石有不同的看法，也很正常，比如“双重运输系统”，我就从来不点，这玩意儿没什么用，还不如多安排几个搬运工，“搬运车”较之都有用得多了。

但是今天看到制作组砍了城市规划，我不免开始担心，如果制作组开始琢磨游戏平衡性的问题——尽管这完全没有必要，而且瞎平衡往往削弱玩家的体验——那实在有太多东西可以砍了。“香料”可以砍，“真菌指南”可以砍，“搬运车”可以砍，“蒸汽烹饪”可以砍。我可以列一大堆东西，理论上能够达成“超模”效果，但这就是Roguelike的乐趣所在呀。Roguelike游戏，玩起来本来就是有难度的，一个不小心就会累积挫败感，在这种情况下，还要对玩家进行削弱，实乃下策，归根结底，“教玩家玩游戏”是很要不得的思路，《Slay the Spire 2》前车之鉴，何必效仿呢？

Плюсы:

Do you feel like the early part of a city builder, where you need to carefully balance spending resources and expanding out vs building up, is the best part of the game?

If so, Against the Storm is for you.

The game delivers on exactly what it promises in an interesting and replayable way. Gameplay runs in concentric cycles, where each mega cycle is defined by the length of time before the storm resets everything, within which you will build multiple settlements. Each settlement is on a clock against the queen's impatience as you run through several cycles of years defined by the different phases of the storm.

The constantly changing parameters, defined by the availability of resources, the modifiers on each individual map, the varied species and their differing needs, keep each game feeling fresh and different. Random map modifiers and challenges add extra spice, and there's a huge range of difficulties to work through as you unlock more bonuses and get better at the game.

Well worth checking out, highly enjoyable, you won't regret giving it a try.

The game solves two problems: Settlers-style production chain games stop being fun once you get your town optimised, and rogue-likes can often ruin you due to RNG.

-Resources are generated randomly
-You get a random set of production chain buildings to choose from but you can choose one
-Every production building has multiple recipes, and most recipes have different inputs. So you produce with what you have from what buildings you choose
-You get to select from randomly generated perks from your settlement. They can be pretty powerful and can add great synergy
-Then you get to go discover new random resources and challenges to attempt. The challenges often require outside-the-box thinking to generate the resources to accomplish
-You also get a series of challenges from the Queen over the course of a settlement. Not entirely random, you get to select from three, so you can choose what's more easily doable with your resources and buildings
-Completing challenges rewards more buildings
-You can also buy more perks and buildings from a regular trader
-If you complete enough challenges in time, you win. Eventually the Queen will get fed up with you and you lose. But challenge completion adds time to the timer, so you can absolutely pull off last-minute saves.

What I'm trying to say is that I never feel locked out of victory, since there are just SO MANY ways to achieve my goals. Every time I've failed, it was due to a mistake I made, not the RNG screwing me over. In addition, every successful colony rewards resources to buff future colinies. Think 1% to producrtion speed etc. So even if you don't have a super successful run, you don't leave empty handed.

If you get it on sale it's super cheap, I can reccomend if you like setting up Settlers-style production chains but always end your towns once you get past the hard, setting-up stage.

Розробники взяли уже класичні механіки містобудівництва з акцентом на мікроменеджмент логістичних ланцюгів та додали рогулайт елементи, які змушують акцентуватися на найцікавішій частині жанру — розбудові міста на початкових етапах. Саме цей момент найважливіший: саме тут ти приймаєш найважливіші рішення щодо вибудовування структури та логістики міста; саме тут ти обираєш форму, якої набуде твоє місто. Далі йде методична масштабізація, де ти просто методично збільшуєш виробництво у міру збільшення потреб. І тут роуглайт-елемент відрізає цей етап, змушуючи тебе перемикатись на нове місто, і це прекрасно!

Та окрім цього роуглайт-твіста гра може запропонувати ще безліч усього. Тут і якісно виконані механіки продуктових ланцюгів — процеси налаштовуються доволі гнучко та варіативно, і ніколи немає єдиного вірного ефективного шляху. Але якраз роуглайк елементи не дають засидітися на одній формулі розвитку, бо кожного разу потрібно адаптовуватися під рандом — і це підтримує свіжість геймплею, бо жодне місто ніколи не буде однаковим. Стартовий регіон та його модифікатори, тип мешканців, стартові креслення будівель, квести, ресурси — усе це кожного разу унікальне та по-своєму формує кожне місто.

Аудіо-візуальна частина також бездоганна. Пастельні, дещо мультяшні текстури нагадали мені ВоВ, а музика… яка ж тут прекрасна музика! Це треба бачити-чути — художнє виконання неперевершене, на мій смак!

Загалом, я міг би ще багато вникати в геймплейні та художні елементи цієї гри, але ви краще пограйте самі — гра вартує того на всі 100!

TL;DR The game is pretty imba thereby eliminating meaningful choices. 

This game has a lot of polish and is very well executed in terms of what it is trying to do. What sets this game apart from others in its genre is its building diversity. None of the building options will do everything you want them to do, thereby creating a interesting choice for the player because there is always a trade off. However, the reason I cannot recommend this game is because once you start to figure the meta out, 80% of the game is noise. Food: Porridge is S tier, jerky is B, everything else is awful. Win Con: Winning via villager happiness is ~5x slower than exploration. Traders and Trade Routes are OP and can bail you out of anything. Most meaningful challenges are trivialized because of trading. I love the idea of what the dev is going for here, but the solution to each match is the same.
